title: Israel’s election: Five key things to know
body: Israel’s election: Five key things to know | Israel Election 2026 News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up EXPLAINER News | Israel Election 2026 Israel’s election: Five key things to know High-stakes vote comes as Israel is mbroiled in multiple years-long conflicts, faces growing international criticism and grapples with deepening domestic polarisation. Listen Listen (8 mins) Save Share Israel’s election: Five key things to know on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info People walk past an election billboard showing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with the Hebrew phrase 'We will not surrender' in Tel Aviv, Israel, October 6 [Abir Sultan/EPA] By Stephen Quillen Published On 26 Oct 2026 26 Oct 2026 Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday for legislative elections. The vote, the first since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, is being called one of the most important in its history . Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 US support for Israel continues three years into the genocide in Gaza list 2 of 3 Israel’s deadline to close UK consulate in East Jerusalem nears list 3 of 3 Protesters in Colombia rally against ties with Israel end of list It will determine the direction of Israel’s government as the country remains embroiled in multiple years-long conflicts, faces growing international criticism and grapples with deepening polarisation at home. Here are five things to know about the upcoming election: Which are the main parties and what do opinion polls suggest? Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, whose term lasts four years. There are two main blocs vying to lead the next government. The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and joined by several far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. These include United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas – both conservative religious parties – and Otzma Yehudi and Religious Zionism-Zehut, led respectively by far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. The main opposition coalition comprises four Jewish-led opposition movements – the Yashar party, led by former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, the Democrats, led by former deputy military chief of staff Yair Golan, the Yisrael Beiteinu party, led by former Finance Minister Avigdor Lieberman and the Together alliance, led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and joined by Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid. Advertisement The latest opinion polls published before a ban on new surveys took effect on Friday showed that neither bloc was on course to secure a parliamentary majority of 61 seats. A poll by public broadcaster KAN projected that the opposition alliance would win 52 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu’s bloc, with the remaining seats going to unaffiliated parties, including the country’s two main Arab-majority political lists – Ra’am, also called the United Arab List, and the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Balad and Ta’al parties. However, both the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs have effectively ruled out joining forces with the Arab-led parties for now. The fractured landscape means Israeli parties could be in for tough post-election negotiations to cobble together a governing majority. If those efforts fail, Israel could end up with a minority government reliant on support from parties outside the governing coalition – or potentially head to another round of elections. What are the key issues? Israelis are grappling with a series of domestic and international crises this election cycle. On the domestic front, there is growing demand for accountability for reported security failures, including those leading up to the October 2023 attacks, anger over the growing ultra-Orthodox community’s military exemption and concern over Netanyahu’s repeated efforts to push judicial reforms that critics say undermine Israel’s liberal democratic order. “The secular and liberal opposition factions in Israel feel this election is the last chance to save Israeli democracy and restore the institutions that have eroded over Netanyahu’s successive terms,” Mairav Zonszein, an Israeli-American commentator who is a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. A war-weary public is also weighing how Israel should proceed with its multiple military conflicts, with many voters seeking security and economic stability while remaining resistant to perceived concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon. What makes this election so important? It is Israel’s first election since the October 2023 attacks and comes amid a surge in far-right attitudes and growing divisions over the direction of the country. “Strains of Israeli society had always been given to violence and right-wing rhetoric, but the trends that had always been present had accelerated under the current government,” prominent Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani told Al Jazeera. Advertisement The election also comes as Israel’s international standing has deteriorated, with a host of Israel’s allies sanctioning its illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, and many other nations denouncing the country’s continued attacks in Gaza and Lebanon. When Netanyahu addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 24, dozens of envoys from around the world walked out , some jeering and booing. The outcome of the upcoming vote could determine whether Israel’s next government maintains its approach to the international community or seeks to repair ties. What does it mean for Netanyahu’s political future? Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has led the country for more than 15 of the last 17 years, and a total of 19, faces growing scrutiny at home and abroad over alleged security failures leading up to the October 7 attack, as well as corruption charges he has been battling since 2019. An electoral defeat would also leave Netanyahu more exposed to his ongoing corruption trial, which could ultimately result in a prison sentence if he is convicted. A new government could also affect the prospects of a potential commission of inquiry into the October 2023 attacks and Netanyahu’s political standing as he faces an arrest warrant for war crimes issued by the International Criminal Court. What about Palestinian citizens of Israel? About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election, including Palestinian citizens of Israel, who number about 1.2 million. Meanwhile, roughly three million adult Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem have no say in the government that controls their borders, movement and legal status. Recent polling suggested that the turnout among the Palestinian citizens of Israel could reach 60 percent, with the majority of the votes expected to go the Arab lists, which are the principal representatives of Palestinian citizens of Israel. If turnout reaches 65 percent, these parties could potentially win as many as 15 seats in the Knesset. Campaigners are aiming for 70 percent turnout, which would be the highest in decades and raise the threshold, keeping smaller parties out of parliament. Last month, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the Joint List and Ra’am from the election. Israel’s top court quickly reversed that decision, enabling the Arab parties to stay in the race. However, the court did force Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh to withdraw from the race over an article in which he described the October 7 attacks as “an important historical event”. The role of Arab parties is going to be significant. Both major coalitions have ruled out joining forces with them for now, but without them, neither coalition might be able to form a majority. Netanyahu has repeatedly sought to portray his opponents as potential partners of the Arab parties, claiming that an opposition-led government will seek their support and that only his Likud party can prevent this. Advertisement Joseph Mansour, a former aide to Israeli Knesset member Ayman Odeh, said politically alienating Arab parties is part of Netanyahu’s political strategy, which could allow him to remain in office as a caretaker prime minister if neither coalition forms a majority. “If Palestinian-led party support becomes politically toxic and the opposition falls short of 61 seats, the deadlock itself becomes the latest win for Netanyahu,” wrote Mansour for the Arab Center Washington DC. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Frank Elderson: Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity
body:
Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Frank Elderson Member of the ECB's Executive Board SPEECH Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at COP17 Finance and Biodiversity Day Yerewan, 26 October 2026 It is a pleasure to open the Finance and Biodiversity Day at COP17. The theme of this COP is “Taking Action for Nature’’. We have talked about the need for action for long enough. Now we need to act. Four years ago, the international community adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, setting out a pathway to living in harmony with nature by 2050. The destination is set. The path is clear. But progress has remained limited. And nature has not stood still. It has continued to deteriorate. So we need to accelerate. Tangible progress requires a shift from targets to implementation, from awareness to engagement, from ambition to investment. COP17 must help us accelerate the journey. And finance has a central role to play. That should not come as a surprise: without investment, there can be no transition. But we need to get the economics right. Protecting and restoring nature is not simply spending. It is investment: investment in the natural capital on which our economies depend, investment in resilience, and investment in our future prosperity. That is why Finance and Biodiversity Day matters. When ecosystems falter, the economy is at risk Let me start with a fundamental question: why is nature so important to the economy? We tend to think of roads, bridges and electricity grids as critical assets that serve as the foundation of a modern economy. But there is another kind of infrastructure that we often take for granted: natural capital. Nature provides services without which large parts of our economies could not function. Water keeps our factories and farms running, healthy soils sustain our food systems, forests and wetlands regulate droughts and floods, oceans absorb heat and carbon. The World Bank estimates that as much as half of the world’s GDP relies on biodiversity, natural capital and ecosystem services. [ 1 ] Our own analysis shows that 72% of companies in the euro area depend on at least one ecosystem service. And 75% of euro area corporate lending goes to companies that are highly dependent on at least one ecosystem service. [ 2 ] The message is clear: nature is not peripheral to economic activity. It is fundamental to it. But even as we speak, the foundations of our economies are being depleted at an alarming rate. [ 3 ] When ecosystems deteriorate, firms face higher costs, lower productivity and supply chain disruptions. For far too long, we have treated nature as though it were free and inexhaustible. It is neither. We have mistaken the depletion of natural capital for economic prosperity. We counted the production. We counted the income. But we rarely – if ever – counted the soils depleted, the water systems stressed, the forests weakened or the ecosystems lost in producing it. In economic terms, we have been consuming our capital and calling it income. Nature is already presenting us with the bill. Depleted natural capital is already disrupting production, damaging supply chains and increasing costs. The consequences are already spreading from ecosystems to firms, from firms to balance sheets and from balance sheets into the financial system. This is not a future tragedy on the horizon. It is an economic reality unfolding around us. That is why taking action for nature is not only an environmental imperative. It is an economic and financial necessity because our future prosperity directly depends on it. The natural currency underwriting economic activity: water Water is perhaps the clearest example of what happens when we fail to account for natural capital. For too long, we have allowed our economies to function as though reliable supplies of clean water were an unlimited production input. But an economy cannot negotiate with an empty river, a depleted aquifer or a failed ecosystem. When we withdraw water faster than it can be replenished, we are not creating prosperity. We are fooling ourselves and failing future generations by consuming the capital on which future prosperity depends. Think about this summer’s heat-exacerbated drought conditions throughout Europe: major rivers, like the Rhine, Loire, Po and Danube, reached exceptionally low levels, forcing, among other things, the shutdown of critical nuclear power plants, while also negatively affecting hydropower and disrupting supply chains. [ 4 ] Drought also contributed to the severity of wildfires. These are not glimpses of a distant risk. They are stark signs of ecosystems already being pushed beyond their limits, with consequences that are already being felt by people and the economy. Unfortunately, our analysis suggests that the potential consequences could be much larger. Research involving the ECB, the London School of Economics and Oxford University has found that a 1-in-100-year drought event could put up to 24% of euro area economic output at risk. [ 5 ] Clearly, too little water is only half of the story. Too much water can be equally problematic. Nearly 12% of economic output in the euro area faces risks from insufficient flood protection. [ 6 ] The recent catastrophic events in Nepal and Bangkok are a stark reminder of the devastating human consequences alongside the destruction of infrastructure and economic assets. And there is a third dimension to consider: polluted water. Take PFAS, for instance. Known as “forever chemicals”, these pollutants are in a wide range of everyday products from textiles and cookware to batteries and food packaging. As the name suggests, they last an extraordinarily long time – and when they leach into the environment, they can be extremely damaging for people’s health and for entire ecosystems, all of which also comes at substantial economic cost. The European Commission estimates that, if current levels of PFAS pollution in Europe continue until 2050, the cost to society could reach €440 billion over that period. Treating polluted water alone could cost more than €1 trillion. [ 7 ] The economic challenge comes from water in all its dimensions: too little, too much, too hot, too dirty. And the effects differ across regions and sectors: agriculture here, manufacturing there and energy production somewhere else. When sufficiently widespread or persistent, the impacts can ultimately affect growth and inflation. Nature: our first line of defence against the climate crisis But the example of water also reveals something else: climate and nature cannot be separated. Healthy ecosystems act as our first line of defence against global heating and related extreme weather events. Europe is the fastest-warming continent. Temperatures have been rising by approximately 0.56 degrees Celsius per decade since the mid-1990s, more than double the global average. This summer again brought record temperatures, following on from 2025 which was the third-warmest year on record, and 2024, the warmest ever – so far. The interplay between temperature, the water cycle and soil quality illustrates why the climate and nature crises should be treated as a nexus. And perhaps nowhere is this more evident than in the ocean. The ocean is one of our planet’s greatest shock absorbers. It has absorbed around 90% of the excess heat from global warming and around 30% of global carbon dioxide emissions. [ 8 ] That is an extraordinary capacity. But extraordinary does not mean unlimited. Even the strongest buffer has its limits. And those limits are no longer theoretical; we are already breaching them. Seven of the nine planetary boundaries have already been transgressed. We are moving increasingly outside the safe operating space on which our economies and societies depend. [ 9 ] In other words, we are consuming the buffers that protect us from economic disruption and climate shocks at precisely the moment when those shocks are intensifying. Nature – an investment in economic resilience and prosperity Recognising nature as economic infrastructure has another important implication. If degrading nature can weaken our economies, preserving and restoring it can strengthen them. This matters particularly today, when maintaining prosperity, resilience and economic security has taken centre stage in the policy debate. Protecting nature is often framed as if it comes at the expense of competitiveness. However, that frames the problem backwards. As we seek to strengthen prosperity and economic security, nature should be seen as part of the solution rather than as part of a separate, often neglected, environmental agenda. Economic security depends on ecological security. Secure water supplies, resilient food systems, functioning ecosystems and reliable energy systems are strategic assets that reduce vulnerability to future disruptions. We should therefore stop treating investment in nature as a competing claim on prosperity and economic resilience. [ 10 ] It is investment in the productive capacity that makes lasting prosperity possible. There can simply be no lasting prosperity on a collapsing natural foundation. We cannot impoverish nature and expect our economies to flourish. Therefore, preserving and restoring nature is not simply an expenditure. It is an investment. We can invest in preserving and restoring natural capital now. Or we can pay increasingly through disrupted production, adaptation, reconstruction and lost economic capacity later. Nature will impose the adjustment regardless. The question is whether we manage that adjustment, or allow it to be imposed on us. From awareness to action So what does this mean for central banks and banking supervisors? Nature-related risks are global and systemic. They do not stop at borders, and no single jurisdiction can address them alone, which makes international cooperation more indispensable than ever. The current geopolitical fragmentation puts global cooperation at great risk. Encouragingly, the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) shows that international cooperation is alive and can deliver. Bringing together 152 central banks and supervisors across more than 95 countries, alongside 24 observers, the NGFS has over time produced several reports that have helped us to develop common methodologies on risk assessment frameworks, supervision and legal risks. [ 11 ] A recently released compendium of good practices [ 12 ] covers 35 examples of how members assess the physical and transition risk impact of nature-related risks, together with six detailed case studies. In other words, the work of the NGFS has helped lay the groundwork for many of the central banks and supervisors now taking action to account for nature-related risks in their core activities. But the NGFS cannot do this alone. Nature-related financial risks need to remain firmly on the international financial agenda, including at the Basel Committee, the Financial Stability Board and the IMF. At the ECB, this shift from awareness to action is already well advanced. Because nature degradation can affect price stability, financial stability and the safety and soundness of banks, nature-related risks are increasingly part of the bread and butter of our work. In banking supervision, we expect banks to identify and manage not only material climate risks, but also nature-related risks, as part of ensuring banks remain safe and sound. [ 13 ] And our recently updated compendium of good practices shows that banks are increasingly doing just that, with around one-third of the practices relating specifically to nature. [ 14 ] Take price stability, for example. We have found that increases in food prices following extreme heatwaves and droughts are an upside risk to price stability. [ 15 ] Nature risks have therefore featured explicitly in our monetary policy assessment and communication in recent quarters. [ 16 ] Nature is not becoming a feature of central banking because central banks are becoming environmental policymakers. Quite the contrary: we are – and will remain – climate and nature policy takers. Nature is becoming a feature of central banking because the consequences of its degradation are affecting our mandate. Conclusion Let me conclude. Four years have passed since Kunming-Montreal. Nature has not waited. We have developed frameworks, methodologies and tools. But while our understanding improved, the underlying ecological crisis has continued to deepen. Today, 75% of land ecosystems and 66% of ocean ecosystems have been damaged, degraded or modified. Humanity is consuming natural resources around 1.7 times faster than ecosystems can regenerate them. The challenge is no longer simply getting to the destination. It is getting there fast enough before the road towards it disappears. Doing so will require investment at unprecedented scale. Protecting and restoring the natural infrastructure on which economic activity depends will require mobilising substantially greater private capital flows towards nature-positive investments, alongside public finance. [ 17 ] But the longer we delay restoring natural capital, the more costly and difficult restoration becomes. And that brings me back to the purpose of today’s event. I would like to leave you with three key questions that I hope will reverberate throughout this Finance and Biodiversity Day. First, how can we mobilise public and private finance at the scale needed to turn the Kunming-Montreal goals into reality? Second, how can governments, financial institutions, international organisations and other stakeholders work together to help turn nature-positive opportunities that are not yet bankable into investments that can attract capital? And third, how can policy, investment and partnerships help to mobilise finance for projects that generate public goods without direct revenue flows? Kunming-Montreal set the destination. COP17 must now accelerate the journey. Turning awareness into action. Turning targets into tangible results. Turning ambition into investment. Because nature is not waiting. Neither can finance. World Bank (2025), Mainstreaming Nature into World Bank Macroeconomic Models: Overview Report , Washington, D.C. Boldrini, S. et al. (2023), “ Living in a world of disappearing nature: physical risk and the implications for financial stability ”, Occasional Paper Series , No 333, ECB. Recently, the Deutsche Bundesbank published a study that shows the German banking sector is particularly highly dependent on ecosystem services linked to water . 75% of land surface ecosystems and 66% of ocean ecosystems have been damaged, degraded or modified. Around 80% of arable land worldwide is affected by soil erosion, salinisation and biodiversity loss. These pressures are projected to reduce global food productivity by 12% by 2040, increasing food prices by up to 30%. We are running an ecological deficit by using natural resources 1.7 times faster than ecosystems can regenerate them. A landmark report by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform , published this year and approved by more than 150 member governments, warns that biodiversity loss is among the most serious threats to businesses. The exceptionally low water levels of the Rhine this summer, the lowest since records began in 1880, have not only disrupted transport and industrial production. They could also reduce Germany's economic recovery by up to 0.2 percentage points of GDP in the third quarter. See Ceglar, A. et al., Nature at risk: Implications for the euro area economy and financial stability , Occasional Paper Series , No 380, ECB. See Ceglar, A. et al., ibid. See the European Commission’s web page on PFAS pollution . See the United Nations web page The ocean – the world’s greatest ally against climate change . See the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research’s web page on Planetary Boundaries – defining a safe operating space for humanity . For example, UNEP estimates that every dollar invested in integrated climate change and air pollution action generates around $15 in economic benefits. This would boost global GDP by 2.8% by 2035 and 4.5% by 2050. Against this, implementation costs are expected to amount to around 0.7% of global GDP in the coming decade. See NGFS (2023), Nature-related Financial Risks: a Conceptual Framework to guide Action by Central Banks and Supervisors ; and NGFS (2026), NGFS 2026 Nature Package . NGFS (2026), Water scarcity as a nature-related financial risk: Legal aspects . NGFS, 2026, Nature-related risks: a Compendium of Implementation Practices to guide Action by Central Banks and Supervisors . Today, more than 90% of the banks supervised by the ECB consider themselves to be materially exposed to climate and nature risks, and all have put in place the foundational frameworks needed to identify, assess and manage these risks. While banks have made substantial progress on climate risk, nature-related risks remain considerably less mature. For example, two-thirds of banks do not systematically link their materiality assessment on nature-related risks to a risk management response, and only a few have defined nature-related key risk indicators. Where such indicators exist, they are often used solely for monitoring, with no limits or thresholds to trigger management action Elderson, F. title: US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls
body: US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls | US Midterm Elections 2026 News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up US Midterm Elections 2026 News | US Midterm Elections 2026 US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls Judge questions the Trump administration’s efforts to exert greater influence over elections process ahead of the upcoming midterm vote. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Election workers process mail-in ballots at the Registrar of Voters facility in San Diego, California, US, on October 23, 2026 [Mike Blake/Reuters] By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters Published On 26 Oct 2026 26 Oct 2026 A United States appeals court has expressed doubt over the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California, which seeks to force the state to throw out mail-in ballots it has deemed likely to go to noncitizens. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said on Sunday the three-judge panel would issue a decision as soon as possible, following a rare weekend oral argument. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rolls list 2 of 3 US judge blocks federal operations seeking to identify non-citizen voters list 3 of 3 Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections? end of list But Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, voiced concern that the lawsuit would not hold up to scrutiny. He pointed to the Elections Clause in the US Constitution, which allows states — not the federal government — to administer elections. “It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department lawyer Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?” The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections. On October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm races, the Justice Department issued a complaint targeting California, a left-wing stronghold. It asked the federal court system to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots that the government says were sent to “likely noncitizens”. The lawsuit indicates the Trump administration sent California officials a list of 20,000 names it believes are not eligible to vote, based on citizenship. Trump has often pushed the discredited claim that the Democratic Party is benefitting from widespread voting by noncitizens. Advertisement California has long been one of the targets of his election misinformation. Earlier this year, Trump denounced the state’s primaries after right-wing candidates like Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt felt short of his expectations. “There’s BIG cheating by the Dumocrats in California,” he wrote on social media at the time. He then announced that the state would be under investigation by the US Attorneys’ Office. Trump’s efforts have caused alarm, with critics accusing him of seeking to dampen voter turnout through intimidation and confusion. The midterms will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local positions. Polls, however, predict steep odds for Republican candidates, given Trump’s souring approval ratings and dissatisfaction with issues like the cost of living and the US-Israel war on Iran. Voting rights advocates have warned that the Trump administration has not publicly revealed how it has compiled its list of noncitizen voters, and whistleblower reports have cast doubt on the accuracy of such lists. In response to the October 15 lawsuit, California has countered that it has strong safeguards to prevent noncitizens from voting. It also said the Justice Department’s claims are based on dubious data. “This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” California Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement earlier this month. “We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook.” aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Ballon d’Or 2026 predictions: Yamal, Mbappe and Kane – who will win?
body: Ballon d’Or 2026 predictions: Yamal, Mbappe and Kane – who will win? | Football | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up Sport | Football Ballon d’Or 2026 predictions: Yamal, Mbappe and Kane – who will win? The winner of the 2026 Ballon d’Or will be crowned at Monday’s gala in London, the first time it’s been held in Britain. Listen Listen (4 mins) Save Share Kane vs Yamal vs Mbappe: Who will win the 2026 Ballon d’Or? on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Harry Kane (left), Lamine Yamal (centre) and Kylian Mbappe are the top three contenders for the Ballon d'Or [File: Getty Images] By Al Jazeera Staff Published On 26 Oct 2026 26 Oct 2026 The race for the 2026 Ballon d’Or is heating up with less than 24 hours to go before the winner is announced at a glitzy ceremony in London. A three-way contest between Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe and Harry Kane leads the debate in the run-up to football’s most prestigious individual honour. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 ‘A match like no other’: El Clasico awaits a Yamal vs Mbappe showdown list 2 of 3 FIFA’s Infantino touts global re-election support amid resignation questions list 3 of 3 Bayern say coach Kompany ‘stable’ in hospital but will be out for weeks end of list Yamal, Spain’s 19-year-old prodigy, and France’s 2018 World Cup winner Mbappe have both publicly endorsed themselves for the honour, while the unstoppable Kane of England has been relatively shy in campaigning for himself. Predictions are pouring in thick and fast as we inch closer to the award ceremony at the London Palladium. Ballon d’Or predictions: Who has AI picked as the winner? According to data released by Avisia, a French data analysis and artificial intelligence firm, Yamal is the favourite to win the 2026 Ballon d’Or. The Barcelona winger is tipped to have a 23 percent probability of lifting the trophy, awarded to the best footballer of the 2025-26 season. The data and AI consulting firm chose Kane as a close second, with a 21 per cent probability, while Mbappe ranked third at 19 percent, tied with Rodri, the 2024 Ballon d’Or winner. The top five list is rounded out by Lionel Messi given an 18 percent chance to win for a record-extending ninth time. Avisia claims it correctly identified the top five for the 2025 Ballon d’Or , won by Ousmane Dembele. Even though Yamal is Avisia’s top pick, it is Kane who the bookmakers see as the outright favourite, with about 70 percent probability. Harry Kane has been in exceptional goal-scoring form for both club and country [File: AFP] What are the predictions of players and experts? Atletico Madrid manager Diego Simeone thinks his compatriot Messi, who recently retired from international duty , deserves to lift the golden ball. Advertisement “After the World Cup, he played at his age… No doubt about it,” Simeone said. Former Italy international Marco Materazzi echoed those thoughts. “With all due respect to Yamal, I think Messi showed, at 38 years old, he’s in a different league,” he added. Lionel Messi guided Argentina to the 2026 World Cup final four years after winning in Qatar [File: AFP] Jude Bellingham, also shortlisted for the Ballon d’Or, backed England captain Kane and his attacking partner at the 2026 World Cup. “He works so hard for it, and he’s a very honest and hard-working person,” Bellingham said. When asked if Kane could win, he added, “It’s definitely possible”. Fellow England international Anthony Gordon sided with his Barcelona teammate Yamal. “What Lamine has achieved at such a young age… the kind of player he is, is ridiculous. He’s on a whole other level,” said Gordon. Mbappe, on the other hand, has the backing of his Real Madrid teammate Aurelien Tchouameni, who said the Frenchman had “an incredible season”. Kylian Mbappe was La Liga and the Champions League’s top scorer in 2025-26 [File: Angel Martinez – UEFA/UEFA via Getty Images] Yamal, Kane or Mbappe: Who will win the Ballon d’Or? Looking purely at individual statistics, Mbappe leads the race as La Liga’s top scorer with 25 goals and the Champions League’s leading marksman with 15. Mbappe, furthermore, also won the World Cup’s Golden Boot and set the record for most World Cup goals (12). Those staggering statistics make him a strong contender alongside Kane, who scored an incredible 73 goals last season – the most by any player since Messi netted 82 in 2011-12. But Mbappe failed to win a trophy with either club or country, while Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern but guided England only to a third-place finish . The lack of major titles weakens their case. This is where Yamal stands out. The youngster won the World Cup with Spain and La Liga with Barca , even though on the personal front, his statistics weren’t the greatest, with injury marring his campaign. Recent history suggests that winning a title in one of the major tournaments has become almost a prerequisite. Only four of the previous 19 Ballon d’Or winners failed to lift any of the Champions League, World Cup, European Championship or Copa America during the year they were honoured. That bodes well for Yamal, who is bidding to become the youngest winner, hoping to surpass Brazilian Ronaldo, who was 21 when he won in 1997. Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal won two major trophies last season [File: Jorge Guerrero/AFP] aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Seoul ‘fabricated’ landmine blast, North Korea tells UN in letter
body: Seoul ‘fabricated’ landmine blast, North Korea tells UN in letter | Border Disputes News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Border Disputes Seoul ‘fabricated’ landmine blast, North Korea tells UN in letter South Korea blames Pyongyang for September landmine blast, but North Korea says incident a ‘sinister obstructive move’. Listen Listen (2 mins) Save Share Seoul ‘fabricated’ landmine blast, North Korea tells UN in letter on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Tourists use binoculars to view North Korea from an observation post in the Demilitarized Zone in Paju, South Korea, on May 25, 2024 [Jae C Hong/AP Photo] By AFP Published On 26 Oct 2026 26 Oct 2026 Pyongyang has sent a letter to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) accusing Seoul of fabricating a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers, according to North Korea’s Korean Central News Agency. The North Korean permanent representative to the UN wrote to the UNSC on Sunday regarding the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 South Korea invites North for military talks over border list 2 of 4 Kim Jong Un crosses new bridge linking North Korea and China list 3 of 4 North Korea to resume propaganda broadcasts, South Korea urges dialogue list 4 of 4 China-North Korea border bridge may do little to spur trade, experts say end of list Tensions have intensified after South Korea blamed a September 21 explosion in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) separating the two countries on North Korean landmines. North Korea has rejected the accusations. Pyongyang’s UN representative alleged the landmine incident was “a sinister obstructive move to brand as a ‘military invasion’”, adding that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”. North Korea’s ongoing border fortification efforts were “a legitimate and just exercise of its sovereignty going in strict conformity with the UN Charter”, the letter states, while also criticising South Korea for violating the charter by firing warning shots at soldiers in the DMZ. South Korea has said it fires shots to make North Korean soldiers return to the north when they cross the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) that runs through the DMZ. In recent years, North Korean personnel have been building tactical roads and fences near the MDL. A barbed-wire fence is seen near the Demilitarized Zone in Paju, South Korea, on June 11, 2024 [Chung Sung-Jun/Getty Images] The South Korean Unification Ministry said on Monday that Pyongyang’s letter aims to “justify its border fortification work” and serve as a “countermeasure” to Seoul’s message to the UN, the Yonhap news agency reported. Advertisement Last week, South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent a letter to the president of the UNSC, casting blame on North Korea for the landmine blast and calling it a “clear violation of the armistice agreement”. The United States-led UN Command also said mine placement by North Korea violated the Armistice Agreement, signed in 1953 to end hostilities in the Korean War. Days before North Korea’s letter to the UN, South ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Korea’s ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Defence Ministry proposed military talks to Pyongyang to “mutually confirm the precise location” of their border to reduce the risk of accidental clashes. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election
body: Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election | Elections News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Elections Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election Leftist president mounts stunning comeback after unexpected first-round loss galvanised supporters of Flavio Bolsonaro. Listen Listen (7 mins) Save Share Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva greets supporters in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25 [Tuane Fernandes/Reuters] By Al Jazeera Staff Published On 26 Oct 2026 26 Oct 2026 Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s contentious presidential race, pulling off a remarkable comeback after a first-round loss that galvanised the country’s political right. Shortly after 9pm Brasilia time on Sunday (00:00 GMT), Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court called the race for Lula, who had earned more than 51 percent of the vote. More than 64 million ballots were cast for the incumbent. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Brazil’s Lula, Bolsonaro draw thousands to election-eve rallies list 2 of 3 Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro about even ahead of election run-off: Poll list 3 of 3 What to know as Brazil prepares for tense presidential run-off end of list Bolsonaro, meanwhile, netted 48 percent, or north of 59 million ballots. More than 4 million votes separated the two candidates, with the final votes still being counted. Coughing and audibly hoarse, Lula took to a flag-draped podium shortly after to give his victory speech. He acknowledged clashes ahead, including with his legislative agenda. “I do not choose the Congress,” he said, citing the legislature’s rightward tilt. “It was the people who chose it, and it is with them that I will vote, work and get things approved.” He also thanked the voters who cast their ballots “to secure democracy in the country”. With his victory, Lula has made history. No other politician in modern Brazilian history has lost the first round of a presidential election only to win the second. “A historic turning point for democracy,” Edinho Silva, the head of Lula’s Workers’ Party, posted on social media, along with a video of supporters chanting, “Ole, ole, ole, ole, ola! Lula, Lula!” But Bolsonaro has so far refused to concede, teeing up a likely court battle over the legality of a Supreme Court decision to extend the voting time by two hours. Advertisement “It is impossible to acknowledge the result,” Bolsonaro said in a short speech, accusing the Supreme Court of having “changed the rules of the game mid-game”. He added that he would seek an annulment of the results. Tumult in the voting process Leaders across the Western Hemisphere, particularly on the left, applauded the result. “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil have won,” Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote in the wake of the results. “Congratulations, President Lula!” United States Senator Bernie Sanders likewise offered his felicitations, calling Lula’s re-election “extraordinary”. “Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers & democracy — and will continue to do so in the next four years,” Sanders said in a statement . Still, the vote process was marred by allegations of voter suppression after reports emerged that public transport in some areas had been suspended. Lula’s allies accused Bolsonaro’s supporters of reducing bus availability in an attempt to dampen the president’s working-class base. Heavy rains, meanwhile, affected southern areas considered to be Bolsonaro strongholds. The campaigns of both Lula and Bolsonaro ultimately petitioned the Supreme Court for a voting extension. Polls across the country were kept open two hours later than expected, until 7pm Brasilia time (22:00 GMT), following a ruling from Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin. Bolsonaro, however, has argued that some polling stations were not able to reopen in time, harming any additional votes he may have earned. A left-wing victory Sunday’s victory means Lula will retain the presidency of Latin America’s largest country, denying a crucial victory to the region’s right wing. In recent years, right-wing leaders have swept presidential races in nearby countries like Peru, Colombia, Argentina, Bolivia and Ecuador. Many have ridden a wave of anti-incumbent energy and enjoyed support from US President Donald Trump, who returned to office in January 2025. A former union leader for metalworkers, Lula – at age 80 – will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, when he will beat his own record as the oldest Brazilian president to take the oath of office since the country’s return to democracy. His victory has earned him an unprecedented fourth non-consecutive term. Lula came into Sunday’s run-off as an underdog. While he narrowly led pre-election, the first round of voting on October 4 showed him trailing Bolsonaro. He earned 45 percent of the first-round vote, compared with the right-wing senator’s 47 percent, both tallies short of the 50 percent needed to avoid a run-off. Advertisement But in the weeks since, Lula has rallied supporters around cost-of-living issues. He championed a constitutional amendment passed this month that shortened the Brazilian workweek, and floated the possibility of providing free public transport on weekends. Having entered politics in the 1980s, during the twilight of the country’s military dictatorship, Lula has run for president seven times. He won two consecutive terms from 2002 through 2010, as well as a third term in 2022, in what was the tightest race in modern Brazilian history up to that point. His rival in that election, former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, is the father of Senator Bolsonaro, Lula’s adversary in this race. Jair Bolsonaro has since been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in plotting a coup following his loss to Lula. Despite overseeing a decline in poverty and low unemployment during his third term, Lula has faced questions about his advanced age, his ability to combat crime, and the country’s polarised political landscape. An explosion of household debt has also left many Brazilians feeling their economic circumstances have worsened. In September, Lula banned online gambling and sport betting apps to address the issue. Uncertainty ahead While the victory over Bolsonaro cements Lula’s status as one of the most significant and influential figures in Brazil’s modern history, efforts to advance legislative priorities during his fourth term could be stymied by the most right-wing Congress in recent memory. There are also questions about how Bolsonaro’s right-wing base and the Trump administration might react to Lula’s re-election. Already, Bolsonaro has suggested he would seek to nullify the election, citing the prolonged voting hours. “What happened today was not normal. It was, in fact, unacceptable,” Bolsonaro told his supporters. Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, also suggested there had been judicial malpractice as a result of the extension. “If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause,” Trump Jr wrote on social media. The Trump White House has been openly supportive of the Bolsonaro family, issuing 50-percent tariffs last year on certain Brazilian products in a push to end the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro. Judges involved in the case were also subjected to US sanctions, most notably Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Lula has framed such manoeuvres as an attack on the sovereignty of Brazil’s judicial system. One of Trump’s critics, US Representative Ro Khanna, suggested the US president could take further actions against Brazil in response to Sunday’s vote. “People all across the world are fighting back against extremism. With Lula in Brazil, they just won,” Khanna wrote . “Trump must respect the results and not undermine Brazil’s elections.” aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Data centre debate heats up ahead of US midterms - here's what you need to know
body: Data centre debate heats up ahead of US midterms - here's what you need to know Published 2 hours ago By Daniel Thomas and the Visual Journalism Team Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was. These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking. They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude. But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world. In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development. It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows. Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing. They are growing rapidly There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map , external , a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites. That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000 , external operational sites. As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead. Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas. But when it comes to actual capacity, the US is ahead by a much larger margin, with China in second place and Europe lagging far behind. This gap is set to widen in the coming years, leading some to warn Europe risks missing out on the potential economic benefits of the AI boom , external . They are getting bigger Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land. The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches. However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows. All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services. For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia. It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution , external . Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards. They use more electricity than France The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages , some experts say. Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows. This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows , while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices . With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam. Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections . Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico , France, Indonesia and the UK . But they can boost jobs But supporters say data centres are critical to national security , and the development of AI. They also say they are good for the economy , external , attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction. A recent report by the Brookings Center , external suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim. The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found. But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits. As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues. This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn , external ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year. But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives. One idea is to put data centres in space , external or on the Moon , where they could harness abundant solar energy. Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones , reducing the need for vast data centres altogether. Additional reporting and design by Erwan Rivault, Matt Faraci and Dominic Bailey. Related topics Artificial intelligence

title: Rapper Nicki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally
body: Rapper Nicki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally Figure caption, Moment Nicki Minaj joins Trump on stage at Michigan rally By Max Matza Published 7 hours ago Rapper Nicki Minaj said US President Donald Trump has "changed the energy of the country" as she joined him at a Michigan rally to stump for Republicans ahead of the nationwide midterm elections. "He's given us a future to look forward to," she said, after Trump praised her figure and called her on stage to speak. Minaj has called herself Trump's "number one fan" despite criticising some of his policies in his first term. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is locked in a tight race with Republican Mike Rogers with just over a week to go before the midterms.  Former President Barack Obama held a rally - one of the first in this cycle - with the Democrat on Saturday. Democrats are also aggressively hitting the campaign trail, with close elections taking place on 3 November which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency. In his remarks on Sunday, Trump focused on El-Sayed's Muslim faith and background, alleging that he will "invite jihadists" into America if he wins. El-Sayed has criticised similar remarks by Trump as Islamophobic, saying in an ad to voters last week that the US president "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office". In Port Huron on Sunday, Minaj, wearing a gold-coloured Gucci-branded suit, led the crowd in chanting Trump's name, and the names of Republican candidates in Michigan. "We really need all these great people to be elected, because this is a major turning point for our country," she said. "She never looked more beautiful," Trump said as she left the stage. "She gets it. She's smart," he added. Earlier in his speech, Trump praised the rear end of one male Republican candidate before turning the crowd's attention to Minaj. "By the way, I looked at a beautiful ass before," he segued. "Nicki Minaj. That's hard to miss." He then asked her to "stand up" as the crowd cheered, and added that he hoped she was not "insulted" by his remark. Image source, Reuters The Super Bass singer had accompanied Trump to the state aboard Air Force One. She filmed a video with an aide - which was posted to X -on the president's plane,  pretending to be interviewing for the White House press secretary role. The position is currently open after Katie Zacharia left five days after a shaky public debut. The Trinidad and Tobago-born rapper has thrown her star power behind Trump a few times before, including on his allegations that Christians face persecution in Nigeria and his "gold card" visa, which offers applicants residency and a path to US citizenship. Related topics Michigan Nicki Minaj US midterm elections 2026 More on this story Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections Published 1 day ago Michigan Senate debate spotlights increase in anti-Muslim rhetoric as midterms race heats up Published 9 October

title: Thousands protest in Prague against public media funding reforms
body: Thousands protest in Prague against public media funding reforms | Politics News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Politics Thousands protest in Prague against public media funding reforms Demonstrators allege Prime Minister Andrej Babis and his coalition’s proposed reforms pose a threat to press freedom. Listen Listen (2 mins) Save Share Thousands protest in Prague against public media funding reforms on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Tens of thousands of people protest against the government's proposed reforms to media funding in Prague, on October 25, 2026 [Gabriel Kuchta/Getty Images] By AFP and AP Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Several thousand people have taken to the streets in Prague to protest against plans to change the funding system for the Czech Republic’s public media, accusing the government of stifling press freedom. On Sunday, protesters demanded the withdrawal of legislation seeking to abolish household licence fees and replace them with state budget allocations for public radio and television. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Czech public media staff strike, citing government threat to independence list 2 of 4 ‘They try to break us’: Pro-Palestine activists in Czech custody list 3 of 4 Czech police detain Russian priest over ‘white substance’ find list 4 of 4 EU to sustain Radio Free Europe with emergency funding after Trump cuts end of list The Czech lower house of parliament approved fast-tracking the bill in a rare overnight vote on Saturday after governing coalition lawmakers rushed to open the issue, limiting the opposition’s ability to engage in debate before the vote was held. The bill, proposed by the governing coalition led by billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis , which includes two far-right parties, must still be passed by the upper house before becoming law. The opposition has pledged to challenge the legislation in the constitutional court. The plan would cut funding for public media by about 15 percent, possibly as early as next year. Czechs protest against a parliamentary vote to approve public media reforms in Prague, Czech Republic, on October 25, 2026 [Gabriel Kuchta/Getty Images] At the protest in Prague’s Old Town Square, demonstrators chanted, “We’ve had enough”, “This must not be allowed to pass”, and “4:36”, referencing the early morning hour when the draft was approved by parliament. Babis has said the plan is not an attack on media independence but a matter of funding transparency. Critics warn the proposed change would allow the governing coalition to take control of the media. They compare it with the actions of populist governments , such as Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico. Advertisement Babis and his coalition, whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine as it fights off a Russian invasion, have a record of attacks against the media. Public media staffers announced they would go on strike on November 3. They are backed by labour unions, university rectors, churches, international media organisations and many others. A rally is also planned at Prague’s Letna park on November 15, two days before the anniversary of the 1989 anti-communist Velvet Revolution that ended more than 40 years of totalitarian government. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Bulgaria election heads to a run-off amid low voter turnout
body: Bulgaria election heads to a run-off amid low voter turnout | News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up News Bulgaria election heads to a run-off amid low voter turnout Bulgarians will now choose between President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov next week. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Bulgaria election heads to a run-off amid low voter turnout on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Presidential candidate and incumbent President Iliana Iotova votes in Sofia, Bulgaria, on October 25, 2026 [Spasiyana Sergieva/Reuters] By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Bulgaria’s presidential election is heading to a run-off after polls closed with low voter turnout and no candidate passing the required threshold. Incumbent President Iliana Iotova received between 35 and 36.5 percent of votes on Sunday , according to exit polls. She will now face former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who scored between 31 and 33.5 percent, in a second round on November 1. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Netanyahu’s pitch: Can Israel use crypto to evade economic sanctions? list 2 of 3 Eight killed in Gaza as Israel targets university campus and other sites list 3 of 3 Serbia’s Vucic concedes election defeat to student-led movement end of list Minister of Interior Ivan Demerdzhiev said the elections “took place peacefully, without the usual practices of vote buying and vote manipulation”, Bulgarian National Television reported. The NATO and European Union member state saw 27 presidential candidates run in the election. A run-off was expected, as turnout must reach more than 50 percent of registered voters, and the candidate must secure more than 50 percent of the votes to win in the first round. Voter turnout was 22.2 percent as of 8pm local time (18:00 GMT), according to the Measure polling agency. Black Sea attacks Rising energy costs, inflation, attacks in the Black Sea and Russia’s war in Ukraine were the major issues in the lead-up to the vote. A series of drone strikes on ships off Bulgaria’s coast, condemned by both candidates, dominated headlines during the campaign period. Leftist Iotova is backed by Prime Minister Rumen Radev, whose Progressive Bulgaria party enjoyed success in April’s parliamentary elections. Iotova became president in January after serving as vice president. A former member of the European Parliament and a journalist, she ran as an independent with the backing of both Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party. Advertisement Should she win, she is expected to keep Bulgaria in line with Europe, while calling for improved relations with Russia. After casting her vote, Yotova said she wanted to address “the dire issue of poverty” in Bulgaria, as well as “inequalities and regional disputes”, the AFP news agency reported. “I believe that there must be peace, stability, and security,” she added. Presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov speaks during a campaign event in Plovdiv, Bulgaria, on October 21, 2026 [Valentina Petrova/AP] Gyurov has the support of the country’s pro-Western opposition and signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine as prime minister. He said on Sunday that he wanted “a Bulgaria that looks forward, a country that is European, free, and proud”. “Next week, Bulgaria must choose between two personalities, two directions,” he said after the vote, and invited Iotova to a debate before the next round. Although the role of president is largely ceremonial, the president leads the armed forces, can veto legislation and sign treaties. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1 at Camp Nou to halve gap to La Liga leaders
body: Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1 at Camp Nou to halve gap to La Liga leaders | Football | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up Sport | Football Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1 at Camp Nou to halve gap to La Liga leaders French superstar Kylian Mbappe scores a brace for Madrid to inflict Barcelona’s first domestic defeat of the campaign. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1 at Camp Nou to halve gap to La Liga leaders on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Real Madrid's Eduardo Camavinga in action before Kylian Mbappe scores their second goal [Albert Gea/Reuters] By AFP Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Kylian Mbappe struck twice to earn Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid a 2-1 El Clasico victory over La Liga leaders Barcelona at Camp Nou, cutting the gap to three points. French superstar Mbappe opened the scoring before half-time on Sunday, then slotted home late on to inflict Barca’s first domestic defeat of the campaign after Raphinha had equalised for the champions. Real Madrid remain third, behind Atletico Madrid and Hansi Flick’s Barca, who had won their first nine games before a chastening week. The Catalans suffered a second straight defeat after losing against Paris Saint-Germain on Tuesday in the Champions League. Barca won six of the seven previous Clasicos since the German arrived, but were surprisingly subdued against Mourinho’s side. “In general, we didn’t have a great game. In the first half, we weren’t ourselves; there were a lot of things we could have done better,” Barcelona midfielder Pedri told DAZN. “We wanted to win the Clasico in front of our fans, but the season is very long… a league is not won here.” Los Blancos, without suspended winger Vinicius Junior, won their fifth straight game across all competitions, and are finding their footing under veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho. After two trophyless seasons, Madrid turned back to Mourinho to try to stop Barca’s dominance, and this result will give them hope they are on the right track. The opening period of the game was cagey, with few opportunities. Barca defender Pau Cubarsi twice reacted well to shut down Mbappe, while Real Madrid’s Marc Cucurella took a rapid liking to Lamine Yamal’s shirt, constantly grabbing at the 19-year-old winger. Advertisement Anthony Gordon, playing in his first Clasico since joining Barcelona from Newcastle, back-heeled the ball to Raphinha, who fired narrowly wide as Barca threatened. The hosts were dealt a setback when young defender Xavi Espart pulled up hurt and needed to be replaced by Alejandro Balde before the half-hour mark. Andriy Lunin, playing in goal for Madrid after Thibaut Courtois pulled out of the squad with flu, saved at his near post from Gordon before the visitors took the lead. Mbappe scored his 10th league goal of the season and also his easiest, with Barca’s Gerard Martin clearing a cross straight at the Frenchman, who deflected it into the net. Barca responded by carving out a glorious chance for an equaliser, but teenage sensation Yamal, for once, miscued in front of goal, firing wide when poised to level. The game opened up, and Yan Diomande came close to doubling Madrid’s lead before half-time, drilling into the side netting. Martin redeemed himself early in the second half as he held off Jude Bellingham, who could neither beat the defender nor find a free Mbappe. Raphinha, who had a quiet first half, pulled Barcelona level just after the hour mark. Pedri fed the Brazilian, La Liga’s top goalscorer with 13, who fired through Bellingham’s legs, and Lunin could not keep the shot out. The Ukrainian goalkeeper did make a superb save to deny Martin a corner as Barcelona flowed forward with the wind finally in their sails. Yamal bent an effort wide with Lunin at full stretch, and Barca substitute Frenkie de Jong had a shot desperately blocked by Dean Huijsen. There was a sting in the tail for the Catalans, though, as substitute Gabriel Jesus lost possession and Madrid raced through on goal. Eduardo Camavinga beat Cubarsi and unselfishly cut the ball back for Mbappe to tuck home his second of the night into an empty net, with Joan Garcia drawn out of position. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history
body: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history Close Israeli voters are preparing to head to the polls in an election some have described as the most consequential in the country's history. It's the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. Tuesday's vote could see Benjamin Netanyahu's almost two-decade-long period of right-wing rule replaced by a more left-leaning government. Emerging as Netanyahu's main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, who says the election is about Israel's identity as a liberal and tolerant democracy. Netanyahu has made security central to his campaign, warning that electing his rivals would risk making Israel less safe. Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.
