title: Marine Le Pen vows French ‘renaissance’ as far right eyes seat of power
body: Marine Le Pen vows French ‘renaissance’ as far right eyes seat of power | Elections News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Elections Marine Le Pen vows French ‘renaissance’ as far right eyes seat of power National Rally’s Le Pen launches presidential campaign against the backdrop of mass protests and social and economic discontent. Listen Listen (8 mins) Save Share Marine Le Pen vows French ‘renaissance’ as far right eyes seat of power on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Far-right party National Rally (RN) candidate in France's 2027 presidential election Marine Le Pen, flanked by RN President Jordan Bardella, right, and far-right ally party Union des droites pour la Republique (UDR) leader Eric Ciotti, left, at a campaign kickoff rally in Orleans, central France, on October 25, 2026 [AFP] By Virginia Pietromarchi Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Orleans, France – Marine Le Pen took to the stage with a clear message: She would lead France’s “renaissance” as the country sank into crisis – and she would do so soon. The far-right figure’s words were met with cheers from thousands of supporters gathered in Orleans in central France on Sunday, as she launched her presidential campaign against a backdrop of mass demonstrations and widespread social and economic discontent. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 France’s far-right National Rally gains ground in Senate vote list 2 of 3 French protest violence: A ‘Christmas present’ for Le Pen’s far right? list 3 of 3 Deadly ‘racist’ attack in France: Are hate crimes rising in Europe? end of list “Marine présidente!” the crowd chanted, waving French flags beneath a sea of red and blue lights. Organisers said 8,500 supporters had gathered in a venue transformed into a fort for the event. Standing tall on stage in a pink blazer, her hair impeccably coiffed, Le Pen spoke with the confidence of a leader who believes the presidency is within reach. Riding high in the polls, with candidates from the right, left and centre trailing behind her, she presented the election as a historic opportunity to restore France’s past glory. “This is a story to be written, a destiny to be fulfilled,” she told the crowd, which erupted in cheers. Her pitch was a promise to restore authority and security in a country she portrayed as having lost control. “We are going to re-establish the rule of law,” she said, drawing loud applause from supporters wearing “Marine présidente” T-shirts. Manon Funeau, 21, a business school student, was among the supporters. “What they propose are values that resonate with me, that vibrate within me,” she said. “Honestly, I feel at home here.” Le Pen’s speech comes as the country is at a crossroads. France has been shaken by a wave of protests since mid-September, a movement sparked by high school students in a Paris suburb that grew into a nationwide mobilisation tapping into widespread discontent. Over the past two weekends, largely peaceful protests have been accompanied by episodes of violence on a scale rarely seen in recent years. Advertisement On October 17 , shops were looted and ransacked, and more than 2,000 people were arrested as hundreds of thousands took to the streets of French cities. A similar dynamic unfolded the following weekend , though on a smaller scale. The protests show little sign of abating, with calls for further demonstrations already circulating. The unrest has given Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) an opportunity to play one of its favourite cards: presenting itself as the guarantor of law and order. It has fuelled criticism of President Emmanuel Macron over his handling of public security, allowing Le Pen to accuse him of incompetence and the far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon – a contender in the coming elections – of encouraging the violence. ‘My country is drifting off course’ “I believe that my country is currently drifting off course,” said Nadede, a 56-year-old who began voting for RN in 2024 over what she said was the country’s growing lack of security. She did not spell out any specific event. “I think that the only person capable of setting it back on the right track is Marine Le Pen – especially since, up until now, everyone else who has run for office has struggled to do so,” she said. Outside the convention hall, the scale of the security operation offered a glimpse of the tensions surrounding the event. Police checks began at departure stations in Paris and continued on arrival, while officers in full gear moved through train carriages during the journey. Orleans itself had been brought to a near standstill. All businesses were shut and public transport suspended. Standing almost alone in the city’s main square was the statue of Joan of Arc, surrounded only by fences. A day earlier, about 3,000 police officers had been deployed to prevent unrest as anti-RN protesters gathered against what they say is a xenophobic and racist party. Orleans was no casual choice. For a party that has long sought to cast itself as the guardian of French identity and national sovereignty, the city is inseparable from the story of Joan of Arc, the 15th-century heroine who helped lift the English siege of Orléans in 1429 and became a symbol of France’s resistance and liberation. For decades, the far right has claimed her as an emblem of national pride, invoking the image of a warrior who came to save France from foreign domination. Le Pen herself has drawn parallels between Joan’s mission and her political ambitions. Eric Ciotti, Nice mayor and president of the Union des Droites (UDR) parliamentary group; French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, member of parliament from the French far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally – RN) party and candidate for the 2027 French presidential election; and Jordan Bardella, president of the RN party, stand on stage during a rally to launch the presidential campaign, after the party’s Congress in Orleans, France, October 25, 2026 [Nicolas Economou/Reuters] The crowd at the RN Congress offered a glimpse of how the party has expanded its appeal to a wider section of society: from young people from urban centres to middle-class workers who used to vote for the centrist party. Advertisement Only a few years ago, the party was still considered on the fringes of French politics. Its growth has been driven in part by a carefully crafted strategy known as dédiabolisation , or de-demonisation, developed over the past two decades to broaden the party’s base while tempering its rhetoric and distancing it from positions that had made it toxic to many voters. The party has long been associated with racism, xenophobia and anti-Semitism. Le Pen’s father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, was convicted of hate speech, including for describing Nazi gas chambers as “a detail of history”. He was expelled from the party in 2015. Far right ‘gaining ground’ Marine Le Pen has sought to broaden RN’s appeal, combining restrictive immigration policies with promises of social protection. The party has gained ground in working-class areas traditionally associated with the left, including former Communist strongholds, by presenting itself as a defender of public services and the purchasing power of everyday people. While RN has long abandoned some of its most radical proposals, including leaving the Eurozone and pursuing a fully fledged “Frexit”, the election of such a eurosceptic to the helm of the European Union’s second-largest economy would send shockwaves. She has pledged a referendum to challenge the primacy of EU law over migration policy, as well as an annual 11-billion-euro ($12.3bn) reduction in France’s contribution to the bloc. The party’s membership has nearly tripled, with approximately 112,000 members now paying their dues, up from fewer than 37,000 in 2022. “The party has been gaining ground at every level: mayors, deputies, senators. Usually, when a movement seems on the rise, people join,” said Baptiste Roger-Lacan, a historian and political analyst with a focus on far-right parties in Europe. “It also shows how it is less and less socially damaging to be a member of the RN.” But the party’s programme “is still fraught with fiscal absurdity”, Roger-Lacan said. “They still want to implement racist laws, which are bound to provoke widespread anger, and their diplomatic agenda is still pro-Russian and anti-EU – even if they don’t advocate Frexit any more.” Jordan Bardella, Le Pen’s second-in-command and Le Pen protégé – an impeccably dressed 31-year-old who looks like a cross between the Wolf of Wall Street and Superman’s alter ego, Clark Kent – also spoke at the event. “No one should be intimidated by their political opinions,” he said, speaking ahead of his mentor. Some observers say the October 17 protests and their aftermath have proved a gift to RN, allowing the party to not only reinforce its law-and-order message but also to shift attention away from recent difficulties. In September, investigative outlet Mediapart published allegations that Bardella had expressed anti-Semitic views in private messages dating back to his teenage years. He denied the allegations and announced legal action against the journalists. The episode posed a challenge for a party that has spent years trying to shed its xenophobic image and recast itself as a supporter of Israel. Advertisement Bardella has also reportedly differed with Le Pen over the party’s economic agenda and whether to make her proposed ban on the wearing of the Islamic headscarf in public spaces a central campaign issue. Yet, at the Congress, those tensions appeared to have been set aside, at least publicly. “Marine president – a Bardella government” was the slogan, projecting unity as Le Pen launched her presidential bid and Bardella positioned himself as her prospective head of government. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit
body: US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit | US Midterm Elections 2026 News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up US Midterm Elections 2026 News | US Midterm Elections 2026 US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit The Department of Justice has faced criticism that its lawsuit is aimed at blocking a Democratic victory in a key race. Listen Listen (7 mins) Save Share US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info US President Donald Trump walks past Attorney General Todd Blanche at the White House on October 21 [Alex Brandon/AP Photo] By Al Jazeera Staff Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 United States Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the Department of Justice’s decision to sue to prevent the certification of a Republican loss in Alaska’s tight Senate race. On Sunday, Blanche did a tour of the morning political shows in the US, making stops at CNN’s State of the Union TV programme and CBS’s Face the Nation. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Trump’s approval ratings plummet: what that means for the US midterms list 2 of 3 Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaska list 3 of 3 Dan Sullivan vs Dan Sullivan: Why is Trump’s DOJ suing in Alaska? end of list In each appearance, he faced pointed questions about the legality of the Justice Department’s efforts, responding, in some cases, with open frustration. “ Why is this controversial?” Blanche asked CNN host Dana Bash at one point. He proceeded to accuse one of the candidates in the Senate race of intentionally trying to confuse voters. “We’re going to try to create a situation where that can be remedied,” he said. “That shouldn’t be something that is causing this shock and horror.” But the Justice Department’s lawsuit , filed on October 22, has been the subject of bipartisan criticism. Many have accused the administration of President Donald Trump of laying the groundwork to block a Democratic win in the race. Trump himself claimed to have authorised the lawsuit. “I’m the one who said do it,” he told reporters on Friday. Inside the Alaska Senate race During the midterm elections on November 3, citizens in Alaska will vote in one of the closest Senate races in the country, which will help decide whether Republicans maintain their majority in the chamber. Senator Dan S Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is seeking to defend his seat in the US Senate. But he faces fierce competition from former US Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat. Advertisement Also in the running is another candidate named Dan J Sullivan, a former Forest Service employee. The second Sullivan’s decision to run has raised concerns that he is a spoiler candidate, whose presence on the ballot is designed to draw votes away from the incumbent. But the Forest Service worker has denied any such intent. Such allegations, he said, are “entirely false”. “I am not a registered Democrat, and I have had no conversations whatsoever with the Peltola campaign about my candidacy,” the second Sullivan wrote in a letter to Alaska’s lieutenant governor before the state’s primaries. “I have considered running for political office for over a decade. I made the decision to formally run for the United States Senate in the upcoming primary election because Senator Sullivan has routinely failed the people of Alaska, and they deserve a better representative. It is my right to do so.” Four candidates advanced to the final round of voting after Alaska’s August primaries. They included Peltola and both Sullivans. The two men are running as Republicans. A controversial lawsuit The Justice Department has argued that its lawsuit – filed less than two weeks before the midterm elections – is necessary “to protect the integrity” of the election. Any result in the Senate race, it argues, would be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan”. The department has therefore called on the US District Court in Alaska to issue an order declaring the race’s certification “unlawful” and barring the state from “allowing such a certification to occur”. Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections, though Congress has the right to pass regulations concerning federal votes. It is highly unusual for a presidential administration to inject itself into issues of state election certification, and experts say such a move is likely to be deemed illegal. Already, in June, Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled that both Sullivans could compete in the Senate race. The state’s Division of Elections has also taken steps to reduce voter confusion. The November 3 ballot, for instance, will list Dan S Sullivan as the incumbent and as a “registered Republican”. Dan J Sullivan, meanwhile, will have the suffix “Jr” added to his name, and his party affiliation will be left blank, despite the candidate identifying as Republican. But in Sunday’s television appearances, Blanche — who leads the Department of Justice and formerly served as Trump’s personal lawyer — argued that merely having two Sullivans on the ballot is a recipe for confusion. Advertisement “It is wrong,” Blanche told CNN. “Putting aside whether we’re going to win or lose in the courts, putting aside what the Alaskan Supreme Court has done, in our system, we should not have a candidate who has to worry about another candidate being on the ballot for no other reason than to confuse voters.” Blanche also denied any impropriety in Trump saying he ordered the lawsuit. “He’s supposed to make sure that everything in this country is running right, including elections,” Blanche said. The race for the Senate Historically, the Justice Department has embraced a norm of judicial independence, though critics have accused the Trump administration of wielding its prosecutorial powers for political gain. Bash, the CNN host, raised some of those concerns, pointing to Trump’s comments accusing Democrats of cheating, as well as his history of election denialism. The president has long denied his loss in the 2020 presidential race, and his supporters sought to block the certification of that election, notably by storming the US Capitol on January 6, 2021. When Bash pointed to that incident, Blanche chided her: “Oh, you’ve got to stop it with that.” “Why are you yelling at me?” Bash responded as the two talked over each other. “You are not being a real person. Come on, man,” Blanche continued. “That is crazy.” He also denied that Trump was setting the stage for a contested election if the Democrat Peltola were to win. Instead, he framed the lawsuit as setting the stage for further investigations into any eventual results. “The relief that we’re seeking – which, again, isn’t to determine who the senator is, it’s not to try to overturn something the state is going to do – it’s just to make sure that the ballots that come in are kept in a way that may allow a court to investigate further,” Blanche said. Speaking to CBS, Blanche also dodged a question about whether Trump personally asked him to file the lawsuit. “I will never, ever, ever talk about communications that I have with the president of the United States. I never have, and I never will,” Blanche said. The race to control the US Senate is expected to be a nail-biter, with Republicans holding a slim majority at present: They have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber. Only a third of the Senate’s seats – 35 in total – will be up for grabs in the midterm races, as terms in the chamber last six years and are staggered across different election years. Trump’s Republican Party is projected to face an uphill battle to protect its congressional majorities, amid backlash against the rising cost of living and Trump’s own withering poll numbers. Roughly seven Senate elections are considered toss-ups, including the Alaska race. In early October, The New York Times and Siena College released a poll finding Peltola leading the incumbent Sullivan by nearly 7 percentage points, one of the widest margins of any of the toss-up states. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Serbia's Vučić concedes election defeat to student-led protest movement
body: Elation across Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić concedes to student-led protest movement Figure caption, Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian streets as Vučić concedes election defeat By André Rhoden-Paul and Jaroslav Lukiv Published 25 October 2026 Updated 1 hour ago Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to the student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections. "We still do not have final results... it is clear that we have lost these elections," the right-wing populist leader said as he conceded late on Sunday. Preliminary figures from Serbia's election commission indicated a record high turnout, which commentators had suggested would favour the student movement. Celebrations erupted after Vučić conceded. Vučić called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence. Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lost Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017. The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state." He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny". There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off.  "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle." During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians  had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added. Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous". "We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, An aerial photo shows the size of the celebrations by Students' List supporters at  Slavija square in Belgrade Vučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade. The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told the BBC Serbian. The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia. It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ilija Srdanović, Student List's leading candidate, pictured during celebrations late on Sunday The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control. Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption. Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare. Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission suggested a record high turnout, with 64.9% having cast their vote by 18:00 local time (17:00 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close. Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia. This was also the case outside booths in number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US. In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris. The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade. Related topics Serbia Belgrade More on this story Joy and disbelief on Serbian streets as Vučić concedes election defeat Published 3 hours ago

title: Can Carrick survive Man United’s slump and Fernandes fallout?
body: Can Carrick survive Man United’s slump and Fernandes fallout? | Football | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up EDITOR'S ANALYSIS Sport | Football Can Carrick survive Man United’s slump and Fernandes fallout? Manchester United cheers Michael Carrick off after Bournemouth loss but booed Bruno Fernandes, what now for crisis club? Listen Listen (6 mins) Save Share Can Carrick survive Man United’s slump and Fernandes fallout? on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes [File: Phil Noble/Reuters] By Kevin Hand Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Manchester United manager Michael Carrick left the Old Trafford pitch on Sunday to the sound of his name being sung by the adoring home support, but he may never lead the team onto the field again. His players followed him and the message delivered to them and the club captain Bruno Fernandes, who was an unused substitute, was quite different. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 All to know about the Ballon d’Or awards 2026 list 2 of 4 Jordan FA chief says AFC Congress ‘pure politics’ at behest of Infantino list 3 of 4 Ronaldinho’s comeback with Ravenna at 46 set for next month at Forli list 4 of 4 Lionel Messi receives top Spanish award in recognition of social work end of list The 3-0 thumping by Bournemouth was a result that marked a 40-year low for the crisis club and plunged it to new depths – and the fans were determined to let United’s owners and playing staff know it. The opening seven league matches marked United’s worst start since 1986. The latest defeat, their sixth of the season, leaves the club just a point above the relegation zone and without a win in eight matches in all competitions. What is happening with Bruno Fernandes and Michael Carrick? Fernandes, the Professional Footballers’ Association’s Player of the Year last season, was left among the substitutes on Sunday as a result of criticising Carrick after Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation at Como in the UEFA Champions League. The Portuguese player has been the Red Devils’ darling since he arrived in 2020, and seemed to have sealed his place as a club legend in a time of darkness with his accolade achieved on the back of United’s third-place finish, which they have only twice bettered in 13 years. The award came as a result of his record number of assists in a Premier League season – all the more impressive in a side that lacked a spark anywhere else on the pitch. Advertisement The upturn in fortunes under Carrick’s interim position last term, when he replaced Ruben Amorim in January, resulted in his full-time appointment in the summer. A tenure that may now have run its course, with him and United’s best player seemingly at loggerheads. How have fans reacted to the Premier League giant’s fall? The United fans are famously loyal to their managers and players. Boos for anyone associated with the home side at Old Trafford were relatively unheard of until the last two seasons. Now the boss receiving the adulation on exiting one of world football’s greatest stages – the Theatre of Dreams – may be the one on whom the curtain is being pulled. Fernandes is no villain in this piece, but United’s fans have delivered a clear message directly to the heart of the dressing room – sending it via the player who could do no wrong in the eyes of the supporters will leave the ears of every member of the squad ringing. Enough is enough. Outplayed is one thing, but being outrun and outfought is another. What is the context of Man United’s demise? United’s history has been one of rebuilds and comebacks. They have known difficult days – their most successful manager Sir Alex Ferguson was on the verge of the sack in 1990 before winning the FA Cup and beginning one of the greatest runs of trophy-laden eras in football. Their wait for a league title stretched from 1967 – and the Holy Trinity of George Best, Bobby Charlton and Denis Law – to 1993, when Ferguson’s inspired signing of Eric Cantona ignited glory days even the biggest club in the world at the time had never seen. Now, United are on the edge of a precipice – quite literally if the gap to the drop zone is even to be realistically contemplated. Perhaps United’s cross-town rivals City won’t be the only Manchester club facing relegation this season. That is demise no one is truly considering yet. Is it a case of Carrick or Fernandes for Man United? They are, however, at a crossroads – and the divide between Carrick and Fernandes – his captain, who criticised the tactics that stopped United pressing their Italian opponents in midweek, is likely to see the axe fall on the manager rather than a valuable asset. “Manchester United need to make the change tonight (Sunday),” former England team-mate of Carrick, Jamie Carragher, told British broadcaster Sky Sports when asked if a sacking was needed. “The fans have taken the side of the manager, which is not about him being the manager, it’s about him being a huge figure in United’s history – and those players have done nothing compared to teams of the past. Advertisement “So Carrick is always going to win that fight – and rightly so – with Fernandes, no matter how talented a player he is. “But also United – one of the biggest clubs in the world – are 16th in the table right now and that can’t happen – it can’t continue and Carrick needs to be relieved of his duties. “He wants to be sacked. It’s become untenable. He doesn’t want to be sat in the dugout with those players. “Imagine going into training with Fernandes after not bringing him on? It’s a rancid dressing room. He wants to be put out of his misery.” Gary Neville, former Manchester United defender and team-mate of Carrick’s for club and country, added: “Carrick is popular, but the owners, the sporting department and the players are not. “They will probably make a decision that will disgust United fans, but it is probably necessary. “The club is a mess.” What has Carrick said amid rumours of the sack? The final word of the day belongs to the man in the middle of a power battle that has seen him win the popular vote, but one that is unlikely to sway the United hierarchy. “I take the responsibility,” Carrick said in the post-match news conference. “I totally understand the situation, I’m not expecting anything, I’m carrying on as normal and I love this place.” In something of a reference to dropping the club captain and the response he received from the crowd at the end, Carrick continued: “I always do what I feel is going to be the best for the club, whatever decision is made. “I’ve tried to do everything I can to not be in this position and for a number of reasons, whatever they are, we’ve not been able to stop that happening to the position we’re in. “I’ve always felt that support and always felt that connection with the [fans]. “I have to say it is mixed emotions, I didn’t really expect that from the supporters. The respect that I have for them and for them to show that back meant an awful lot.” Emotions are running high at Old Trafford and, even though Carrick denied it, his fanfare at the end may well prove to have been his farewell. The Theatre of Dreams has become a house of horrors – for the 11th manager since Ferguson retired and with United’s last Premier League title now stretching back to 2013. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Serbia voter turnout highest in decades as students oppose longtime leader
body: Serbia’s Vucic concedes election defeat to student-led movement | Elections News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Elections Serbia’s Vucic concedes election defeat to student-led movement Vucic says the opposition Student List is projected to win a parliamentary majority after nearly two years of protests. Listen Listen (5 mins) Save Share Serbia’s Vucic concedes election defeat to student-led movement on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Serbia's former President Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade on October 25, 2026 [Zorana Jevtic/Reuters] By Al Jazeera Staff and AP Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Serbia’s longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic has conceded defeat to a student-led movement in the country’s snap parliamentary election, saying the opposition group is set to secure a majority of seats. Vucic said on Sunday that, based on a sample of votes, the Student List was expected to win between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with 105 for his electoral list. Recommended Stories list of 2 items list 1 of 2 Serbia votes in election pitting longtime leader against student movement list 2 of 2 Serbia votes as student-led bloc challenges longtime leader Vucic end of list While stating that final results were not yet available, the populist leader said, “It is clear that we have lost these elections.” His announcement was greeted with cheers, euphoria and tears at the Student List headquarters, according to the Belgrade-based FoNet news agency. “Preliminary results show that students are convincingly leading in almost all polling stations,” Radomir Saicic, a parliamentary candidate for the Students’ List, said in a speech at the movement’s election headquarters. “Students won, and with them also a hope that Serbia can be a country of justice, freedom and dignity,” he added. “Let this night be the beginning of a new chapter.” Voting to determine whether Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has governed since 2012, could retain power against a movement born from nationwide anticorruption protests, ended at 8pm local time (19:00 GMT) on Sunday. The State Election Commission said that by 6pm (17:00 GMT), voter turnout had reached 64.9 percent, ⁠⁠⁠⁠the ⁠⁠⁠⁠highest since ⁠⁠⁠⁠the breakup ‌‌‌‌of Yugoslavia in ‌‌‌‌1992. University of Belgrade researcher Jelena Vasiljevic told Al Jazeera in an interview published on Friday that the SNS had a reliable voter base, while the students needed to attract people who normally did not vote. Advertisement Sunday’s voting was also marred by reports of intimidation and procedural problems. The Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA), an independent election watchdog, said its observers recorded pressure on voters or election workers at almost a third of the 500 polling stations it monitored. It also reported failures to protect ballot secrecy. By 5pm (16:00 GMT), the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy (CeSID), an election-monitoring group, had received about 260 reports of potential irregularities, including ballot photography, group voting and difficulties with identification checks. Serbians celebrate Celebrations erupted across Serbia, with fireworks lighting the sky almost immediately after Vucic’s announcement conceding defeat. Tens of thousands crowded Belgrade’s main roads as supporters of the Student List drove around in cars, honking their horns. Serbians chanted, “Aleksandar is gone”, and sang the student movement’s songs. Crowds dismantled tents set up at a park in central Belgrade, where Vucic’s loyalists had been camping for more than a year. “It means freedom from a dictatorship that has lasted for 12 years, that I cannot remember a time before,” voter Jana Vasic told Al Jazeera. “I’m not completely sure what our candidates will do first, but I think first for tonight, we’ll celebrate. And then tomorrow, the real hard work starts.” People in the Serbian city of Novi Sad celebrate in the streets October 26, 2026, after the student movement declared victory at snap parliamentary elections [AFP] Belgrade resident Dragana Kovecevic told the Associated Press news agency that she was thrilled that “everyone greets with smiles”. She added: “We are all too happy; finally, we are becoming one normal and free country.” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated the Student List on its election victory, writing on X: “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.” Pressure from student-led movement In Belgrade, as the election took place, police wearing riot helmets and carrying shields were deployed near the election commission’s headquarters, where roads were closed and barricades erected. City prosecutors appealed on Sunday for everyone involved in the election to avoid violence. The election follows nearly two years of student-led protests that began after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. Demands for accountability widened into a movement against alleged government corruption and repression. Vucic and the SNS deny the accusations. Advertisement The Student List – Students Win, which emerged from demonstrations, fielded candidates drawn from professions including medicine and education, many of whom have no political experience. The movement campaigned for stronger institutions and an end to corruption. Some established opposition parties backed the students rather than fielding their own candidates. Vucic resigned as president in September to run for prime minister, promising higher pensions, public-sector wages and investment. Supporters credit his leadership with modernising Serbia’s economy. About 6.5 million people were eligible to vote for 250 parliamentary seats, with 18 electoral lists competing. A majority of 126 seats is needed to form government. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Will Michael Carrick be sacked? Man United manager says he doesn’t know
body: Will Michael Carrick be sacked? Man United manager says he doesn’t know | Football | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up Sport | Football Will Michael Carrick be sacked? Man United manager says he doesn’t know Manchester United’s 0-3 home loss to Bournemouth has left the 20-time champions winless in eight Premier League games. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Will Michael Carrick be sacked? Man United manager says he doesn’t know on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Manchester United's manager Michael Carrick after losing to Bournemouth at Old Trafford [Darren Staples/AFP] By AFP Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Amid increasing pressure on his team and a growing threat to his own position as manager, Michael Carrick says he will do what is best for Manchester United after a 3-0 demolition by Bournemouth plunged his future into doubt. Winless in eight games in all competitions, the 20-time English champions slipped to within one point of the relegation zone after a damaging defeat at Old Trafford on Sunday. “It’s a tough situation,” Carrick told British broadcaster Sky Sports. “What is next? I don’t know. “I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I’ve said it all along; I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility, but we’ll have to wait and see.” Asked in a post-match news conference if he expects to be sacked in the coming days, Carrick replied: “I totally understand the situation. I’m not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. I’m carrying on as normal. I love this place.” Despite a dismal run of results, the United fans largely supported the former midfielder as he made his way off the field at full-time before they turned on the club’s players. “I have mixed emotions to have that connection with the supporters in the moment we’re in. I need time to digest that,” added Carrick. “I appreciate their support but the situation is where it’s at. We haven’t been good enough.” Manchester United’s captain Bruno Fernandes did not feature in the match against Bournemouth [File: Darren Staples/AFP] Carrick’s decision to drop captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench and not even introduce the Portuguese international as a substitute backfired. Advertisement Fernandes, last season’s Premier League player of the year, had criticised Carrick’s tactics after the 4-1 thrashing by Como on Wednesday. Carrick said before the game that his call was a “pure football” decision, but it was hard to believe Fernandes was not being punished as he was left on the bench for the entire match. “There’s always times in games when you are trying to change the course of the game and to make a difference,” said Carrick as he swerved questions on Fernandes’s absence. “Those were the decisions we made today.” Carrick was appointed on a two-year deal only in May after a successful caretaker spell in charge led United to third place in the Premier League last season. However, he has been unable to arrest the club’s steep decline since his former boss Alex Ferguson retired as manager in 2013. United were outspent by many of their rivals in the transfer market as they added just three midfielders – Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. But Carrick said a lack of investment did not justify such a decline in results. “Last season to finish third was a really good achievement in the circumstances,” added Carrick. “We understood where that left us, what was next, what needed to be done and how we needed to improve, and where we were at as a team and as a group at that stage. “I definitely knew that we hadn’t cracked it and there was a lot of work to be done, but that doesn’t mean to say that it should have gone this way.” aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Uganda orders 21-day Ebola quarantine for citizens returning from DR Congo
body: Uganda orders 21-day Ebola quarantine for citizens returning from DR Congo | Ebola News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Ebola Uganda orders 21-day Ebola quarantine for citizens returning from DR Congo Kampala says country is Ebola free, but Swiss authorities believe a woman diagnosed in Nigeria was infected in Uganda. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Uganda orders 21-day Ebola quarantine for citizens returning from DR Congo on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi arrives for a media briefing on the Ebola outbreak in Kampala, Uganda on October 25, 2026 [Abubaker Lubowa/Reuters] By AFP and Reuters Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Uganda has ordered citizens returning after travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to quarantine for 21 days, as it steps up precautions against the Ebola virus . Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi announced the measure on Sunday at a news conference in Kampala, as Ebola cases in Kenya and Nigeria raised fresh questions about travellers passing through Uganda. Recommended Stories list of 2 items list 1 of 2 Kenya announces second Ebola death, says ‘no evidence’ of community spread list 2 of 2 WHO warns ‘more complex’ Ebola outbreak now present in 3 African countries end of list The country says it has no active infections after ending its own outbreak in July. Returning Ugandans with a history of travel to DRC will have to pay for their quarantine, the Ministry of Health said. Officials have also strengthened checks at Entebbe International Airport and land crossings, and require all incoming travellers to complete forms recording how they can be contacted. Uganda declared its Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak over on July 28. It had recorded 20 infections and two deaths, according to the Health Ministry. Yet Swiss authorities have said a Ugandan-born woman married to a Swiss diplomat contracted Ebola during a visit to Uganda in September. Nigeria confirmed her infection on October 20, after she had travelled to Abuja, its capital. At Sunday’s briefing in Kampala, Baryomunsi challenged that conclusion. He said relatives who had previously visited DRC had met the woman in a Kampala suburb, and questioned whether that possible route of exposure had been ruled out. “We should speak science, not politics,” he said. The World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations’ health agency, said on Thursday that the information it had received did not show that the woman herself had travelled to DRC. Advertisement Nigerian and Ugandan officials are investigating her movements and possible source of infection. The inquiry has also turned to a Kenyan man who travelled from DRC through Uganda before flying to Nairobi on October 3. He died two days later, and Kenya has since reported a second Ebola death. Both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day. Ugandan officials said on Sunday that security footage showed no physical interaction between them. Nigerian authorities said genetic testing found closely related viruses in the two cases, but no direct link had been established. Baryomunsi said 60 people traced in Uganda after possible contact with the Kenyan patient had finished 21 days of monitoring and been discharged. In neighbouring DRC, where the outbreak began in May, the WHO had recorded 9,704 cases and 4,687 deaths by October 20. Ebola, which can cause haemorrhagic fever, has reached eight Congolese provinces, making this the country’s largest recorded outbreak of the virus. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people. The strain responsible for the current outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved vaccine or specific treatment. Symptoms can take up to 21 days to appear, according to the WHO. In its October 23 update, the WHO urged stronger monitoring and cooperation across borders, while advising against restrictions on travel or trade with affected countries. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Protein shakes for teenagers: Good or bad idea?
body: Science Global issues Protein shakes for teenagers: Good or bad idea? Jeannette Cwienk 10/25/2026 October 25, 2026 Protein products are marketed as a way of building muscle and losing weight — and they're very popular with young people. They also claim to promote healthy growth in children. Is this true? How much protein is healthy? https://p.dw.com/p/5Od7R Do we need protein shakes if we do a lot of sport? Image: Monkey Business 2/Shotshop/picture alliance Advertisement You can take it as a powdered drink, or in a snack bar. Puddings and certain breads are also promoted as "sources of protein," and protein-enriched products like Kindershake and Teen Balance are specifically designed to appeal to a young people — and it appears to be working. In a representative survey of almost 1,000 parents by the University of Michigan in 2024, just under half said their children, who were aged 13 to 17, had consumed protein products over the previous year. The survey found that boys were more likely to do so than girls, especially in connection with sport, or to build muscle. Girls took them to balance their diet, and to lose weight. According to the statistics portal Statista, between March 2024 and March 2025 the fitness protein product market in Germany recorded a huge jump of around 25% in retail revenue. How much protein do we actually need? Proteins are key building blocks for our metabolism. They play an important role in building up and repairing tissue in our muscles, skin and organs. Proteins are the basis for the formation of enzymes that regulate chemical reactions in the body, and of antibodies that are vital for our immune system . According to the German Nutrition Society (DGE), healthy adults should consume 0.8 grams of protein daily per kilogram of body weight. A woman weighing 65 kilos should eat 52 grams of protein per day, for example. But they can do this without special protein products. A portion of oat flakes with an almond drink for breakfast, a baked potato with curd cheese for lunch, and two slices of wholemeal bread with peanut butter in the evening — objective achieved. Young people should consume a little more, as they are still growing. For them, the formula is 0.9 grams of protein per kilo of body weight. A teenager weighing 45 kilos should therefore eat 40.5 grams of protein per day. People over 65 and children aged one to four should have a little more: one gram of protein per kilo of body weight. Older people tend to eat too little protein, often because their appetite decreases. But a study done in Germany between 2015 and 2017 showed that children and young people there often consume too much. Around half of six- to 17-year-olds ate more than double the recommended daily amount of protein. Can too much protein be dangerous? Too much protein can be harmful in the long term, according to the DGE. Various studies show that children who eat too much protein, particularly animal protein, often become overweight . Some enter puberty early . Eating too much protein can cause people to become overweight and lead to health problems Image: yurakrasil - stock.adobe.com Above all, too much protein can put excessive strain on the kidneys, causing damage. The kidneys have to convert the amino acids that constitute the building blocks of proteins into urea before they are excreted in urine. Damage is particularly likely if a person doesn't drink enough fluids, or has pre-existing kidney damage — but adolescents are also at greater risk. Protein helps build muscle and shed weight A person's protein requirement is greater if they are very physically active. Among other things, according to a DGE position paper, proteins can help maintain or build up muscular mass and strength, and support recovery after strain. The paper states that, depending on physical condition and what they are training for, sportspeople should consume between 1.2 and 2 grams of protein per kilo of body weight, divided into several portions throughout the day. These recommendations only apply to people who train for more than five hours a day. Proteins are of interest to people who want to lose weight because they are good at satisfying hunger. People usually lose more weight by following a protein-rich diet rather than another. Long-term, though, the most important thing to look at is: How many calories am I consuming, and how many am I burning? Is animal protein better than plant protein? Overall, plant proteins usually contain somewhat fewer essential amino acids than animal protein . "Essential" because the body cannot make them by itself – it has to take them in as food. Vegetarian protein for muscle building To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, wholegrain products, pulses , or nuts are also higher in fiber, vitamins, and unsaturated fats – all of which are healthy. The DGE therefore advises that protein intake should be increased primarily with sources of plant protein . What is the criticism leveled against protein products? Protein powders and bars are often enriched not only with vitamins and minerals but also with unhelpful ingredients like sweeteners , sugar , additives and flavorings. The German Sport University in Cologne even found doping substances in protein products that were praised for building muscle. Adolescents in particular might experience an unpleasant side-effect of consuming protein powders. These usually consist of milk proteins. There are various ways in which milk proteins can increase the skin's production of sebum, and this can trigger or exacerbate acne, although a direct link between milk protein products and acne has not been definitively proven. Protein powder made from whey: Around 200 liters of milk are needed for one kilogram of powder Image: Carballo/Depositphotos/IMAGO Specialists are also skeptical about protein shakes, fearing that they could lead to young people eating fewer normal meals, and thus consuming less fiber, micronutrients , and healthy fats. 'High protein content' = higher price Protein-enriched foods are usually expensive. In a 2022 study, consumer organizations also found that foods that are naturally high in protein, such as cheese, curds, or soya drinks, often cost more if the protein content has been highlighted by the manufacturer. Not even sportspeople with a high protein requirement need to supplement their diet with special protein products. The DGE advises that they should aim to satisfy their requirements by optimizing their diet, and says there is no scientific evidence that our bodies require protein-enriched food supplements when put under strain. However, the experts do say that it may make sense for people to use protein preparations if they have allergies, problems with digestion, chewing, or swallowing, or if their appetite is very low. This article has been translated from German. Advertisement

title: Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation
body: Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation Image source, Getty Images By Aleks Phillips Published 25 October 2026 A man suspected of a deadly gun attack near Paris has left custody and been placed under psychiatric observation, French anti-terrorism officials have said. One person was killed and five others injured on Friday when an attacker opened fire from his car - first in Trappes, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin. The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, will be observed to evaluate whether his "psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing his interrogation", the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said. President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack", adding that people had been targeted over their skin colour or religion. It marked a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation", the French president said. Figure caption, Watch: Emergency services at the scene of the shooting on Friday PNAT said the move to place the suspect under psychiatric evaluation followed guidance from a psychiatric expert. The evaluation will determine whether the suspect should remain in police custody and is "likely to last 48 hours", PNAT added. PNAT said the suspect was also found to have cannabis and cocaine in his bloodstream. French newspaper Le Monde , external and news agency AFP report that a Bible, a Quran and a copy of Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf were found at the suspect's home, citing a source close to the investigation. The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "very rare". He alleged that it was being used to portray the suspect as criminally irresponsible rather than having acted deliberately. Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was named as the one fatality on Saturday. The mixed martial arts club where he trained paid tribute to him, saying: "On the mats as off them, he was one of those who lead by example: present, respectful, always ready to lift others up. "His smile, his energy and his generosity will remain etched in our walls and in our hearts." Three of those injured in the attack were taken to hospital in a serious condition - including a 12-year-old girl who remains in a critical condition. The mayor of La Verrière, Nicolas Dainville, told French radio network France Info on Sunday that he had spoken to the girl's mother over the phone and confirmed she was "doing better". Another injured resident was recovering while a third remained in a critical condition, he said. The suspect had been known to police prior to the attack but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. PNAT previously said he had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged". He is thought to have used an old semi-automatic weapon during the attack, firing in bursts from his car window. title: Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack
body: Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack | Gun Violence News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Gun Violence Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack Jordan’s prime minister represents king at funeral for eight of the church attack victims as hunt for gunmen continues. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info A coffin is lowered during the funeral on Sunday for victims of the church shooting in Karak in Jordan [Alaa Al Sukhni/Reuters] By Al Jazeera Staff , AFP and Reuters Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 Thousands of mourners have gathered for the funerals of eight of the victims of a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan, with Prime Minister Jafar Hassan also in attendance. The burials on Sunday were beside St George’s Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, southwest of the capital, Amman, two days after attackers opened fire during another funeral there. Recommended Stories list of 2 items list 1 of 2 Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan? list 2 of 2 Jordan’s King Abdullah orders firm response after deadly church attack end of list Nine people were killed and dozens wounded in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority, prompting three days of national mourning. The ninth victim, Mohammed al-Qasous, is due to be buried on Monday, his family told the AFP news agency. Coffins wrapped in Jordanian flags were carried through crowds gathered around the church in Karak province, as priests led prayers and security personnel stood guard. Prime Minister Hassan attended the service alongside government ministers and senior military and civilian officials, according to Jordan’s state news agency, Petra. Thousands of citizens also participated in the funeral procession, Petra said. Among those caught in Friday’s shooting was Sahar al-Halsa, who told the Reuters news agency from her nearby home that she sheltered behind a pillar as gunfire erupted and people screamed. When she rushed outside, she found her cousin Assem lying wounded. “Assem, Assem, my darling, answer me,” she recalled calling to him. He briefly opened his eyes before dying, she said. Father Yohanna Hamati told AFP that about 170 to 200 people were at the church for Friday’s funeral when firing began outside. Advertisement The mourners initially struggled to understand what was happening, he said, before people began rushing into the church to escape. By Saturday, bullet holes remained in the walls and wooden pews, and windows had been shattered. Church workers were cleaning away blood as villagers prepared to bury the dead. Jordanian authorities have described the attack as “extremist terrorism”. King Abdullah, who visited some of the wounded in hospital on Friday, has promised a forceful response and the assailants are still being sought. Officials say they have not established whether the attackers were connected to an armed group and no organisation has claimed responsibility. The violence has also drawn expressions of solidarity across religious lines. Christians account for about 3 percent of Jordan’s largely Muslim population and AFP reported that Muslims were among those wounded. Young volunteers visited a hospital in Karak with flowers and a message reading, “Our loss is one”. The mourning reached Washington, DC, on Sunday, where members of the Jordanian community lit candles outside their country’s embassy. Jordan’s ambassador to the US, Dina Kawar, told those gathered that efforts to stir religious division were “bound to fail”. Back in Hamoud, Father Hamati appealed for unity, stressing that Muslims had also suffered in the attack. “We make no distinction between Muslim and Christian,” he told AFP. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement

title: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
body: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban Image source, PA By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 25 October 2026 Gabon says it has lifted a ban on social media imposed eight months ago - a move that triggered widespread criticism at the time. The High Communication Authority (HAC) announced the U-turn on Saturday in a televised statement. The BBC has approached the country's media regulator for comment. The ban had been introduced on 17 February, with the HAC saying that online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions in the country. The move came as a shock to the central African nation of about 2.5 million people, where social media platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram have been particularly popular with younger people who use it for business as well as pleasure. Many turned to VPNs in order to continue accessing social media sites following the ban. The ban had been imposed at a time when the Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema was facing a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election. Teachers and civil servants had staged strikes over what they said were low pay and poor working conditions. The opposition said the suspension was an abuse of power. Nguema won last year's elections with more than 90% of the vote, two years after his coup had ended more than five decades of rule by the Bongo family. At the time he pledged to reform Gabon, a small, oil- and timber-rich country, where digital blackouts were used by the previous governments to control information. Related topics Gabon Social media Africa More on this story Social media suspended in Gabon for 'spreading of false information' Published 18 February

title: Russia to host first Olympic federation world event since Ukraine invasion
body: Russia given first championships since Ukraine invasion Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Weightlifting was first included as an Olympic sport in the 1896 Games in Athens By Craig Nelson BBC Sport Journalist Published 25 October 2026 Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships - the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced its decision on Sunday, four months after confirming Russian athletes would again be eligible to compete in its events. In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted a suspension on the Russian Olympic Committee. That suspension had been imposed following the country's invasion of Ukraine. The IOC's subsequent decision potentially opened the way for Russian athletes to compete for their country at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. The IWF announced the host cities of four world championships at junior, youth and senior levels, awarding the 2029 senior event to Ahmedabad in India. "All the bids we received were excellent and we are sure that the championships in your respective countries will be a huge success," said IWF general secretary Jose Quinones. No world championships in an Olympic sport, summer or winter, have been held in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine. The 2025 World Aquatics Championships, initially awarded to the Russian city of Kazan, were instead moved to Singapore. Moscow has not held the World Weightlifting Championships since 1983. The Russian Weightlifting Federation said: "[We are] the first Olympic sports federation to succeed in bringing a top-level official competition back to the country in many years." Federation president Aleksandr Vinokurov thanked the IWF in a post on Telegram "for their trust", with the championships also serving as a qualifying event for the 2032 Olympic Games in Brisbane, Australia. "Russia has all the necessary experience and capabilities to host competitions of the highest level," he said. "Moscow has repeatedly staged major international sporting events and has modern infrastructure." In announcing its decision in July to provisionally lift Russia's suspension, the IOC said that no decision had been taken on whether Russia could display their flag, colours and anthem at the Olympic ‌Games. The IOC said it would continue to "not organise IOC events in Russia or invite Russian government or state officials to its events". Some Russian athletes competed at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games and this year's Winter Olympics in Milan as neutrals. Ukraine filed an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) requesting that the IOC decision to lift its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee be annulled. The IOC's move decision came after the International Paralympic Committee had already ended Russia's exile from global sports events, with the country's athletes allowed to compete under their national flag at the Winter Paralympics. Five Ukrainian athletes are listed to compete in the 2026 IWF World Championships in Ningbo, China, which are scheduled to take place from 27 October to 8 November. Related topics Weightlifting Olympic Games

title: The search for gold is a dangerous and laborious gamble for Sudan’s miners
body: The search for gold is a dangerous and laborious gamble for Sudan’s miners | Sudan war News | Al Jazeera play Live Sign up Show navigation menu play Live Click here to search search Sign up Features | Sudan war The search for gold is a dangerous and laborious gamble for Sudan’s miners As Sudan’s war destroys livelihoods and pushes people towards artisanal mining, the death of 16-year-old Altayeb Alhadi highlights the dangers facing young workers in an industry offering little protection. Listen Listen (6 mins) Save Share The search for gold is a dangerous and laborious gamble for Sudan’s miners on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Artisanal gold mines have been vital sources of income for thousands of Sudanese [FILE: Mojahid Satti/Al Jazeera] By Al Jazeera Staff Published On 25 Oct 2026 25 Oct 2026 When Altayeb Alhadi was just six years old, his father died after a well collapsed in his village in White Nile state, south-central Sudan. Two months later, his mother also died, leaving the five children in the family as orphans. As the eldest of the siblings, it was Altayeb’s responsibility to find work and help the family survive. At 14, he travelled hundreds of kilometres from his home in Galli village to seek work in the north, where gold mines dot the landscape, so he could feed his siblings and keep them in school. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 At least 72 Sudanese miners killed in air strike: Rights monitor list 2 of 3 Deadly gold mine air strikes highlight Egypt-Sudan border insecurity list 3 of 3 Sudan’s soaring fuel prices make getting by harder for workers end of list “We warned him about the dangers, but he was ambitious. Some relatives were already working in the area although they had found jobs in restaurants and other services rather than underground extraction,” Ayateb’s uncle Alhadi Hamid told Al Jazeera. The boy initially worked in transport and other jobs, but when he heard lucrative stories from miners in the area, he began to search for gold in the surrounding mountains. Altayeb died in an air strike attributed to the Egyptian military at a gold-mining site near Jabal Al-Aigdat in Sudan’s Red Sea region on October 10, which killed at least 72 miners , a few months after he began working at the site. “It was less than 30 minutes since we separated, and he said he was going to the mine. We suddenly heard a loud sound of bombardment, and we ran. It was too chaotic with people running in all directions and many attacks taking place within a few minutes,” a fellow miner told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity. Advertisement “We found Altayeb with his hand and leg [blown off] and a severe injury to his abdomen [which] was open. We tried to help him and took him to a safer place near a mountain. We were terrified. He died within hours. … We couldn’t believe how quickly things could happen.” Dalago market in northern Sudan close to gold mines [FILE: Mojahid Satti/Al Jazeera] Altayeb worked alongside about 15 young men and children, using basic tools to extract gold from the rocks. The miners worked night and day, taking the material they gathered to nearby mills for processing. Proceeds from any gold found were shared, but earnings depended on the amount of gold recovered and individual agreements. On productive days, the group could earn more than $100, the miner said. “We used to dig for two to three weeks until we found a gram or less. If the gold percentage in the well wasn’t good, we would change locations. When we found a gram or less, we sold it and shared the profit, which was about $100,” Altayeb’s former colleague said. For young people supporting relatives, even irregular earnings in these dangerous gold mines can seem preferable to unemployment. Altayeb told his siblings 10 days before his death that he would soon return home, his sister Rogaia Alhadi told local media. Friends told the family that Altayeb visited them at a restaurant near the mining site on the morning of the attack, his uncle said. They shared a cup of tea before heading towards the mine for the final time. Minutes later, the air strike hit the area. An artisanal miner breaking stones to extract gold, Dalago market [FILE: Mojahid Satti/Al Jazeera] Authorities in Egypt have accused Sudanese miners of crossing its border and reportedly linked some to gold smuggling, drugs and human trafficking. The Sudanese side did not respond to these allegations. Since a civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group broke out in 2023, the economy has tanked and forced thousands with no other source of income to find work in the artisanal gold mines of northern Sudan. This can vary from independent prospecting to working in investor-owned pits for a share of the proceeds. Earnings depend on the amount of gold found, equipment and fuel costs, and profit percentages agreed with financiers. Although some miners strike gold, they still face an array of dangers, ranging from collapsing shafts and unstable ground to air strikes. Limited medical care makes mining, particularly in remote areas, especially hazardous. Advertisement Living conditions are also extremely hard. Mohamed Awadalkarim, who was a miner in River Nile state for 10 years, said workers often shelter in makeshift huts made from burlap sacks and plastic sheeting. Their diet consists mainly of lentils and sorghum porridge. But for families without reliable incomes, mining offers a possible source of immediate earnings. Miners may spend hours searching for gold and not find enough to cover their expenses. Others share proceeds with investors or equipment owners, leaving them with limited money left. Artisanal and small-scale mining accounted for 53.71 tonnes, or about 83 per cent, of Sudan’s declared gold production in 2024, but this was just in areas under government control, according to research by the Chatham House think tank. About one million people were involved in artisanal mining across Sudan’s 18 states, generating $1bn annually for the country. An artisanal miner burning gold in Dalago Market, Sudan [FILE: Mojahid Satti/Al Jazeera] Artisanal mines, while generally viewed as being outside the main war-funding networks, have still been exposed to violence. On June 16, several people were reportedly killed and injured in attacks on mining sites near the Egyptian border, according to local sources and miners. The repeated air strikes near Sudan’s border with Egypt have raised concerns about civilian protection, territorial sovereignty and accountability. Egyptian authorities have accused Sudanese prospectors of crossing the border to mine near a concession managed by an Egyptian company, but there is little independent evidence to back these claims. Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan reportedly ordered a fact-finding committee involving prosecutors, judicial representatives and security agencies to investigate the attack. Findings from an inquiry into a similar incident announced in June have not been made public. Altayeb paid the highest price in this regional conflict and the hunt for gold, which provides huge profits for some and meagre incomes for many. Altayeb’s siblings are now living with their extended family, including uncles, aunts and cousins. People who know them are trying to help his brothers and sisters and are carrying out community initiatives in Galli to keep his memory alive. “We will raise the children and care for them as he would have wanted. He was young, caring and brave, and he will always be remembered,” Altayeb said. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement
