title: Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases, but infections in Kenya and Nigeria are prompting fresh scrutiny
body: Health Africa Ebola cases in Kenya and Nigeria raise concern in Uganda Andrew Wasike in Nairobi, Kenya 10/25/2026 October 25, 2026 Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria crossed paths at Uganda's main airport as conflicting accounts cloud the source of one infection. https://p.dw.com/p/5OaQW Both patients are known to have traveled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3 Image: Sumy Sadurni/AFP/Getty Images Advertisement The first confirmed Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria may have crossed paths at Uganda's Entebbe International Airport, according to African health officials, as new information from Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account of the Nigerian patient's travel history. Uganda , a country reporting no active Ebola infections, has become a focus of investigations into cases thousands of kilometers apart. Uganda insists that it has no confirmed active cases of the deadly virus . Yet health authorities in Kenya and Nigeria are investigating Ebola infections involving people whose travel histories or contacts are connected to the East African nation. Both patients passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, according to Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) . Health officials say the two may have crossed paths, although it has not been established whether they encountered each other or whether any transmission occurred at the airport. The differing accounts have raised questions about whether Uganda was simply a transit point for infected travelers. Or could infections be going undetected along some of Africa's busiest cross-border routes? The latest developments come after Switzerland disputed claims that the Nigerian patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) , where an Ebola outbreak is underway. Did the two Ebola patients cross paths in Uganda? Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate confirmed an Ebola case in the capital, Abuja , involving a woman who had recently traveled to East Africa, including Uganda. "Today we are confirming that there has been one imported case of Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory," Pate said. The woman developed symptoms on October 7 and visited a private health facility on October 11. Further laboratory testing confirmed Ebola, and she was subsequently isolated for treatment. Pate said the patient was stable and health officials had identified 44 contacts, including health care workers, caregivers, patients and people who may have encountered her during her travels. But the woman's journey has become central to the investigation. Speaking on Thursday, Mankoula said the first confirmed patients in Kenya and Nigeria were both known to have traveled through Entebbe International Airport on October 3. Investigators are examining whether the two patients were at the airport at the same time and whether their movements overlapped. Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account Uganda's Health Ministry says preliminary findings indicate that the Nigerian patient traveled to eastern DRC for business before passing through Uganda without symptoms and returning to Nigeria. "Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in an October 20 statement. But, on Friday, Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs directly disputed the account. "She and her husband did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the department said in a statement to Reuters news agency. The woman, identified by Swiss authorities as a Swiss national of Ugandan origin, is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja. Ebola cases have now been detected in multiple African countries Image: Afolabi Sotunde/AP Photo/picture alliance On Thursday, the Swiss government told Reuters that she was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling with her husband in Uganda, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC also said Thursday that they had not received confirmed information establishing that the woman had traveled to the DRC. The conflicting accounts raise fresh questions about where the woman was exposed to the virus and how accurately her movements were initially reconstructed. They do not, however, establish that she contracted Ebola in Uganda. Uganda maintains that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says it is awaiting more detailed information from Nigeria about the woman's movements. Kenya's missing contact complicates investigation In Kenya, Uganda has emerged in a separate investigation involving the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, who died in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 5. The patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before reaching Kenya. Health officials have now established that the patient passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, the same day as the woman subsequently diagnosed in Nigeria. Kenyan authorities have since reported additional infections linked to the initial case. But one aspect of the investigation remains unresolved. According to Kenya's Daily Nation , health officials are searching for a Ugandan national identified as a contact of the deceased patient. "We know him (the Ugandan) by name and passport number and from his phone but we are not able to reach him," Kenya's director-general for health, Patrick Amoth, told the newspaper. The Daily Nation reported that the man was using a South Sudanese telephone number, complicating efforts to establish his whereabouts. Being an untraced contact does not mean that he is infected. However, locating potentially exposed individuals is essential to preventing further transmission. Can border screening stop Ebola? Uganda shares a lengthy border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Ebola outbreaks have repeatedly challenged health authorities. Cross-border trade, population movements and international travel make it difficult to establish where someone was exposed to the virus. Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ebola symptoms typically develop two to 21 days after infection. According to the WHO, people infected with Ebola are not considered infectious until symptoms appear. Even well-functioning border surveillance systems cannot identify every infected traveler. The discovery that both patients traveled through the same international airport on the same day illustrates the complexity of tracing potential exposures across multiple countries. It also highlights the importance of reconstructing travel histories and identifying close contacts. Uganda says it is strengthening screening and public health controls at points of entry. Nigeria has intensified contact tracing and infection prevention measures. The challenge is ensuring that authorities across different countries can exchange accurate information quickly enough to identify potential exposures. Anxiety grows in Nigeria In Abuja, the confirmed infection has revived memories of previous Ebola outbreaks. Resident Peace Kolawole expressed concern about the consequences of another outbreak. "So here is my hand sanitizer, so I'm actually very concerned about it," she told DW. Others fear that Nigeria's health care system may struggle to respond while many citizens face economic hardship. "Because now people are not even worried about sickness anymore, people are worried about surviving," Abuja resident Jonathan Steven told DW. Nigeria's health authorities say the patient is receiving medical care and contact tracing is continuing. What remains unanswered? Uganda's position between the DRC and other regional destinations offers one explanation for its appearance in both investigations. But the latest findings have added two significant questions: Did the patients from Kenya and Nigeria come into contact at Entebbe International Airport on October 3? And where did the Nigerian woman contract the virus if, as Switzerland insists, she never traveled to DR Congo? Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The conflicting accounts from Uganda and Switzerland have made establishing the Nigerian patient's travel history an urgent part of the investigation. The WHO and Africa CDC have yet to confirm the disputed DR Congo travel history. Uganda's declaration of zero confirmed active cases does not establish that all infections have been ruled out. Equally, the travel histories do not prove an undetected outbreak. For Kenya and Nigeria, the immediate priority is containing confirmed infections. For Uganda, the challenge is demonstrating that its surveillance systems are effective and reassuring both its citizens and neighboring countries. The Africa CDC will convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials on October 28 as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread. Edited by: Keith Walker Advertisement

title: More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
body: More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France Figure caption, Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishes By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 24 October 2026 Updated 25 October 2026 More than 1,300 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France on Saturday that were followed by some clashes later in the day, officials have said. After largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux. Officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history. The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000. Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them Published 4 days ago Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched. The interior ministry said 53 officers were hurt in clashes across the country on Saturday. French President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, In the southern port of Marseille, protesters erected makeshift street barricades and set them alight late on Saturday Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism. Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", news agency AFP reported. The Interior Ministry said 142 people were arrested in the French capital on Saturday, less than half of the number arrested on the same day last week. Image source, EPA Image caption, Protesters clash with police at a demonstration in Bordeaux In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city. Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux. In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture. "There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city. Nuñez also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France. He said the number of arrests across the country would likely rise. The man in Toulouse, a 20-year-old protester, had several fingers torn off one hand when a nearby explosive went off, Franceinfo reported, citing the medic who treated him. As the unrest continued into the early hours of Sunday morning, authorities in Bouches-du-Rhône, the region in which Marseilles sits, said seven businesses had been "looted or damaged". Image caption, "We really want a change in France," a teenage protester told the BBC Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office. "They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said. Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government. "I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police." He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France". Image source, Reuters Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally (RN) party in the north-central city of Orléans, which proceeded peacefully. The recent unrest has played out against a backdrop of a polarised political landscape, with France preparing for what could be the most divisive election period in a generation. Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest French voters will ultimately face a choice between RN's candidate Marine Le Pen and that of the radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed). Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron, though right-wing figures have also heaped criticism on rioters while left-wing leaders support the union-led protests. LFI candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon said French media had not covered the peaceful protests while police had created "a setup deliberately designed to provoke chaos" that had "mutilated two people". Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday. In Barcelona, more than 120 people were arrested after a student protest descended into what local authorities described as "gratuitous violence". In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels. In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops. Image source, EPA Image caption, People clash with police during a demonstration against the high cost of living in Bordeaux. Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests. Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to AFP, while about 1,000 police officers were injured. The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities. The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers. Related topics France Paris Marseille Lyon Toulouse

title: Gadi Eisenkot campaigns on Moroccan roots in challenge to Netanyahu
body: Politics Israel Can Eisenkot's Moroccan roots challenge Netanyahu in Israel? Felix Tamsut Sderot, Israel 10/25/2026 October 25, 2026 As Israel prepares to vote, Gadi Eisenkot is leveraging his Moroccan heritage in Likud strongholds such as Sderot. From historical divides to October 7, identity and trauma are redefining the city's political loyalties. https://p.dw.com/p/5Obt3 Gadi Eisenkot election ads use the term 'a prime minister of our own' in Moroccan Arabic Image: Felix Tamsut/DW Advertisement Ahead of Tuesday's elections , party advertisements greet people arriving by train to the outskirts of the western Israeli city of Sderot. Campaign posters with various slogans promote the right-wing Likud and the far-right Otzma Yehudit parties. However, one poster is seen more than any others: that of the liberal Yashar party. Its slogan, "Rosh Memshala Dialna," combines the terms "prime minister" in Hebrew and the words "of our own" in Moroccan Arabic. And there is a good reason why Eisenkot's campaign in Sderot and other cities on Israel's sociopolitical periphery focuses on his Moroccan roots. Eisenkot's Mizrahi background Sderot — located in the Negev desert, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) to Tel Aviv's south and just a kilometer away from the Gaza border — is a city with a large Moroccan Jewish community. In recent decades, the city has become symbolic of Moroccan-Jewish culture in Israel, finding its expression in music, cinema and state politics. Israel elections: Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's challenger? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Historically, Sderot is considered a bastion of the Israeli right, and especially a stronghold of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's Likud. In 2022, Likud received more than 40% of the votes in Sderot, compared with 23% nationwide. Other members of Israel's far-right coalition received a lot of support there in the last election. This pattern reflects deeper historical divisions in Israel between Ashkenazim, or Jews of European origin, and Mizrahim, or Jews mostly from Middle Eastern and North African backgrounds. According to estimates, half of Israel's Jewish population is of Mizrahi origin, amounting to about 4 million people. Mizrahi Jews have faced discrimination and neglect since the early days of the Israeli state. This inequality still shapes the economic and social reality in Israel ― and its political discourse. The issue has received special attention in the 2026 campaign. Eisenkot, Netanyahu's major challenger, is of Moroccan origin and grew up in Eilat, a city with a large North African Jewish population. Eisenkot's Yashar party accused Likud of sidelining its Mizrahi politicians. The campaign slogan, "Netanyahu: Let the Mizrahim give interviews,” mocked that omission. A sticker campaign in Sderot called for a Mizrahi prime minister Image: Felix Tamsut/DW On live television, the right-wing journalist Yinon Magal — one of Netanyahu's most vocal supporters — claimed that Eisenkot was being controlled by elitist Ashkenazim and called him a "monkey." Netanyahu, who is of European origin, condemned the remark. Morocco-born Daniel Ben-Simon, an award-winning Israeli journalist and a former member of parliament, told DW that Eisenkot's embrace of his roots might have been forced upon him by Magal's comments — but it has historical value nevertheless. "People don't use terms like 'Dialna' with pride," Ben-Simon said, referring to Eisenkot's embrace of the Arabic term "of our own" in campaign posters. He said Israeli society had long tried to erase the Arab identities of North African Jews. Eisenkot's embrace of his identity serves as a way of "leaving the frame" set by society. "By using such a term, you're creating a new identity: an Israeli-Moroccan identity," Ben-Simon said. "Eisenkot is the first to allow this double identity to be expressed and still feel at home." Israel's historical divide After Israel 's founding, the ruling socialist party, Mapai, whose leadership was largely Ashkenazi, pursued discriminatory policies against Mizrahim. Mizrahim were often expected to "Europeanize” rather than preserve their own culture, heritage, or Arabic language. Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel's election? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video These inequalities also took a material form. In the state's early decades, while European immigrants often received better housing and jobs, many Jews from Arab-speaking countries were sent to Ma'abarot, or temporary transit camps, often in remote areas with little infrastructure. Many later became "development towns,” which remained underfunded compared with Israel's central regions. That in turn resulted in poverty. Sderot, in the south, is one of the best-known development towns. For many Mizrahim, limited access to jobs, education and infrastructure symbolized long-standing exclusion by the Mapai establishment. Likud, founded as a right-wing alliance in 1973, used this frustration effectively under Menachem Begin . Mizrahi support for Begin helped produce the Mahapach, or upheaval, when Likud first defeated the socialist camp and took power. Since then, Mizrahim have often been associated with Likud, even though the party has never had a Mizrahi leader. Sderot's changing demographics Over the past two decades, Sderot's proximity to Gaza has made the city a frequent target of rocket attacks launched by the militant group Hamas . During the Hamas-led terrorist attacks on October 7, 2023 , the city of Sderot was hit especially hard. More than 50 people were killed.  In the three years since the attack, the city's population has grown by about 5,000 people, bringing it to 40,000, with many young families making the town their home, both as a result of idealism and government benefits. The Sderot memorial for the victims of October 7 Image: Felix Tamsut/DW Walking around the town, it's hard not to notice that the so-called national-religious community is becoming increasingly dominant. This community tends to vote for Bezalel Smotrich's far-right Religious Zionism party, a main member of Netanyahu's coalition. Though votes for Smotrich and his party are de facto votes for Netanyahu's bloc, the prime minister's Likud party itself could suffer losses in Sderot. Regardless of the election's results, the perception of Sderot as a city of Moroccan Jews is not bound to change anytime soon. Ben-Simon said Eisenkot's election could serve as an opportunity for reshaping Moroccan Jews' future identity in Israel. "The connection cities like Sderot have to their Moroccan roots would grow stronger as a result of an Eisenkot win," Ben-Simon said. Edited by: Shani Rozanes Advertisement
retained_feed_body: As Israel prepares to vote, Gadi Eisenkot is leveraging his Moroccan heritage in Likud strongholds such as Sderot. From historical divides to October 7, identity and trauma are redefining the city's political loyalties.

title: Prague honors Roma resistance fighters against Hitler
body: Politics Czech Republic Prague honors Roma resistance fighters against Hitler Lubos Palata 10/25/2026 October 25, 2026 More than 1,400 Roma fought against the German Nazi occupation in Czechoslovakia. A new exhibition in Prague showcases the stories of partisans and soldiers whose fates barely received any attention for decades. https://p.dw.com/p/5OW7L Since the end of WWII, the role of Roma resistance fighters was largely unknown Image: Luboš Palata/DW Advertisement For more than half a million Roma in Czechia and Slovakia , October 15, 2026, marks an important milestone. That day, an exhibition on a largely forgotten chapter of Czech history opened at the Museum of the Romani National Revival in Prague. The exhibit explores the role of Czech and Slovak Romani resistance fighters during the Nazi German occupation and the dismantling of Czechoslovakia from 1938 to 1945. Until now, Czech and Slovak Roma appeared in the history of World War II almost exclusively as victims of the Holocaust against Roma and Sinti. In the so-called Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, Nazi Germany murdered approximately 90% of the Czech Roma during World War II. However, what is less well known is that a large number of Czech and Slovak Roma fought against the German occupiers as partisans in resistance groups and as soldiers in the Czechoslovak Underground Army, or Defense of the Nation, ON. The organizers of the exhibition hope that people will bring their children and grandchildren to show that Roma and Sinti have their own heroes Image: Luboš Palata/DW Roma have heroes, too The exhibition at the Museum of the Roma National Movement therefore marks a turning point in how the Roma are viewed during World War II . At least that is the hope of museum director Emil Scuka, a lawyer, former prosecutor and one of the best-known Czech Roma activists. "We were not only victims; we were also heroes," Scuka said in his speech to several hundred attendees at the exhibition opening, most of whom were Roma from Czechia and Slovakia. "Many people, not even among the Roma themselves, are aware that we Roma fought against Nazism," he noted. In his view, "organizing and opening the exhibition was something my generation owed to these Roma heroes and today we are repaying that debt." Scuka called on those present: "Bring your children and grandchildren here so they can see for themselves and realize that the Roma have heroes too!" He also pointed out that this topic had been completely marginalized in Czech and Slovak historical writing for decades and that the Roma had therefore decided on their own to document the fates of their war heroes. The exhibition presents the detailed life stories of 100 of the most significant Roma partisans and Roma soldiers from the Czech underground army and resistance groups who fought against the Nazis. "We found over 1,400 Romani fighters in the archives. From among them, we selected the 100 most interesting stories for this exhibition," said exhibition curator Radoslav Scuka at the opening. Unseen heroes — Sinti and Roma resist Nazis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Groundbreaking research on Roma resistance fighters Among these figures is Anton Facuna, a sergeant in the American intelligence agency Office of Strategic Services (OSS), who was flown to Slovakia in October 1944 on a secret mission. Slovakia had been a puppet state of Hitler from 1939 to 1945. Another is Josef Serinek, known by the nickname "Black Partisan from Vysocina," who managed to escape from the Nazi concentration camp for Roma in Lety and subsequently founded and commanded the large Capajev-Cerny partisan unit in the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands. In 2022, Czech President Milos Zeman posthumously awarded him the Medal for Heroism. Toward the end of his life, Serinek shared his memories with historian Jan Tesar, who later wrote the three-volume book "Ceska cikanska rapsodie", which translates to Czech Gypsy Rhapsody. Except for Tesar's book, the history of Roma resistance against Nazism has not been researched by Czech and Slovak historians to this day. "I am not aware of any scholarly historical work that deals with Roma resistance against Nazism," Prokop Tomek, a historian at the Military History Institute in Prague , told DW. "The number of 1,400 Roma who took part in the fight against Nazism as members of the resistance or in the foreign army does not strike me as an exaggeration and corresponds to the proportion of the Roma population in Czechoslovakia," Tomek said, adding that the "exhibition on the Roma resistance against Nazism during the war is undoubtedly groundbreaking." The life of resistance fighter Anton Facuna is one of around 100 examples on display Image: Luboš Palata/DW Fears of revealing one's Roma identity To this day, many Roma in Czechia and Slovakia do not publicly acknowledge their ethnic identity. This is partly due to experiences with the Holocaust during the Nazi era that have been passed down through generations. Czech historians and politicians continue to debate the extent to which the Czech authorities of the Protectorate were complicit in the extermination of the Czech Roma. However, one thing is certain: the police registration of all Roma, which had been enshrined in law in Czechoslovakia since 1927, facilitated the extermination of the Roma by the German Nazis. According to estimates by the Czech government, approximately 250,000 Roma live in the country today. In the 2021 census, however, only 21,000 people identified as Roma. Of all ethnic groups in Czechia, which has a population of 10 million, the Roma are among the three largest ethnic minorities in terms of numbers. However, they are the most socially disadvantaged, have very little political representation, and are therefore scarcely present in Czech politics. Roma, Sinti persecuted in WWII still fight for recognition To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This article was originally written in German. title: Saudi Arabia looks to US for an AI edge as Yemen's Houthis up pressure
body: Conflicts Saudi Arabia Saudi Arabia looks to US for an AI edge as Yemen's Houthis up pressure Cathrin Schaer 10/25/2026 October 25, 2026 The US is helping Saudi Arabia fight the Houthi group in Yemen with AI-assisted targeting. But AI is not a magic bullet, experts say, and there are technological, political and human rights issues to consider. https://p.dw.com/p/5OYkc Almost 200 people, mostly children, were killed at a school when the US military used AI-assisted targeting in Iran in late February Image: Atta Kenare/AFP Advertisement Under attack from the militant Houthi group in neighboring Yemen, Saudi Arabia has asked numerous allies for help. That includes the United States, even though media report that US President Donald Trump refused when Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman asked him to take direct military action against the Houthis. However the US is providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence, which includes a targeting tool that uses artificial intelligence, or AI. A September report by US broadcaster CNN, quoting several unnamed American officials, said that between 100 and 200 US soldiers were in Saudi Arabia as part of new joint force command to facilitate this. The US personnel were helping the Saudis "use a targeting tool that allows military officers to see in real-time what is happening on the battlefield," CNN reported. Officials said the system in Saudi Arabia was similar to that known as the Maven Smart System, or MSS for short, which the US military has also used as it sought targets in Iran, Iraq and Syria. UK sends warplanes as Saudi Arabia seeks more help against Houthis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What is Maven? MSS came out of what's known as Project Maven, the US's flagship artificial intelligence program for the military, first launched in 2017. MSS itself is an AI-enabled digital platform that "aggregates, organizes and visualizes vast streams of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data," analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington explained in a June text . The software system identifies patterns in data coming from, for example, live satellite feeds or drone cameras and then labels potential targets such as possible rocket launchers, tanks or suspicious vehicle convoys. Previously human military analysts would have had to look at a wide array of different sources to try to find those, the CSIS researchers wrote. It was difficult and, in the case of hours of satellite or drone footage, almost impossible. But MSS now brings hundreds of sources together, analyses them all, then flags possible targets. It also calculates the best method of hitting the target. Tech commentator Bilawal Sidhu, a former Google product manager, has described the MSS set up as like a "Google Earth for war." Using the MSS dramatically speeds up what is known as "the kill chain" — that is, the time it takes to detect a target, decide if it's dangerous and then order a strike. When the US military used MSS while attacking Iran in late February, the AI-powered system facilitated hits on more than 1,000 targets within the first 24 hours of the war. Previously American soldiers were hitting about 100 targets a day. A faster kill chain? Up until recently, the long-simmering civil war in Yemen had been comparatively calm following an informal ceasefire negotiated in 2022. The Houthi rebel group has held large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2015. Yemen's internationally recognized government and other groups held territory across the south and east. That latter is supported by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. The Houthi group has been fighting in a civil war in Yemen as well as against Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states since 2015 Image: Mohammed Huwais/AFP The Houthi's latest military campaign, which began in September, has seen the group take further control of Yemen's coast . They also ramped up attacks against Saudi Arabia again, hitting the country's main airport and oil facilities. So far, though, military campaigns against the Houthi group by Saudi Arabia, the United States and others have all failed to significantly weaken the group. This is partially because the Houthis take a "zero-sum approach," Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House, told DW recently . The group's founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too "soft," and that poverty and hardship are a divine test, al-Muslimi said. "They don't care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital," the expert said. "It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice." MSS's major issues There are certain technical issues users have noted with the MSS in the past that could also prove problematic in Yemen. The Houthis tend to be highly mobile, using truck-mounted ballistic missiles and small drone swarms as they operate from hills and canyons in rugged countryside. It's possible that fighters might be long gone before they can be attacked  even with the help of AI-assisted targeting. Iraq in 2003: During the US invasion of Iraq, about 2,000 US military personnel were responsible for targeting; in a 2024 army exercise using MSS, only 20 were needed Image: Jamal Saidi/REUTERS Though MSS is known to work best in relatively unpopulated areas, factors such as changes in desert terrain, dust storms, high wind, snowfall and dense foliage — and even deliberately planted decoys — can reduce its success rate. There is also a worrying ethical aspect to shortening the kill chain. A human is always supposed to verify the target that the AI-assisted tool has identified and decide how to react. But it doesn't always work that way. For example, among the sites MSS targeted in Iran on the first day of the war was a school. An American missile killed almost 200 people at a primary school in southern Iran, most of them children aged between seven and 12. Could AI defeat the Houthis? In its military campaign in Gaza, Israel — arguably the Middle Eastern country with the most advanced military-use AI — has also used AI-assisted targeting. An Israeli system known as the Gospel, or Habsora, is the closest to MSS in the way it works. But, as has been documented elsewhere, including by Israeli and British journalists and in the recent documentary Naza , the use of such AI targeting tools have also been highly problematic because of the numbers of civilian casualties that can result. The school a US missile hit had previously been part of an Iranian naval base, yet was listed online as a school and playgrounds were visible on satellite imagery Image: Vantor/REUTERS "On the one hand [in Gaza], AI has enhanced commanders' situational awareness, lessened the human costs of tunnel mapping, improved the speed of military strikes, and boosted the survivability of troops," analysts Frederic Wehrey and Andrew Bonney wrote for War on the Rocks , a specialist media outlet. "Yet the benefits afforded by such functions have been overshadowed by mounting civilian deaths reportedly resulting from this technology's safeguards being loosened or eliminated." All of which is why Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist based in Australia who has researched the impact of Israel's AI-assisted technology, doesn't believe similar technology will lead to the defeat of the Houthi group. "I don't think there's much evidence at all that using an AI tool is going to make much difference on the ground, except for causing huge amounts of civilian casualties," Loewenstein, who authored the book, "The Palestine Laboratory: How Israel Exports The Technology of Occupation Around the World," told DW. "And I think what the US and the Saudis will find is that the Houthis have an incredibly high tolerance level for destruction." Edited by: Carla Bleiker Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Advertisement

title: Bulgaria holds presidential elections amid divisions over Ukraine war
body: Politics Bulgaria Low voter turnout in Bulgaria triggers presidential run-off Jon Shelton | Timothy Jones 10/25/2026 October 25, 2026 Low voter turnout has triggered a run-off for the Bulgarian presidency. The vote was colored by strong divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine, and Sofia's relations with the Kremlin. https://p.dw.com/p/5OdWi Despite a few plus ones, voter turnout was historically low in Bulgaria's presidential election Image: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Record low turnout in Sunday's Bulgarian elections mean voters are expected to head to the polls on November 1 to cast ballots in a presidential run-off. Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 8 p.m. (0500-1800 GMT), with official results expected within 48 hours, but voter turnout was less than 40%, far short of the 50% required. Voters were choosing between candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and relations with Moscow and t he vote came as drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast brought home the significance of the conflict in Ukraine for the former Soviet satellite state. Although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the head of state in Bulgaria can appoint interim governments during political crises, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and is able to veto legislation. Bulgarians are deciding on who should officially reside here in Sofia Image: Dzhanan Mehmed Ismail/Anadolu/IMAGO Who are the main candidates in Bulgaria's presidential election? Frontrunner in the elections is incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who took over the position this year after current Prime Minister Rumen Radev stepped down to take part in the parliamentary elections that led him to power. Yotova, 62, who surveys show as having 41-47% of the vote, favors dialogue with Moscow as the way to bring peace to Ukraine and opposes military aid to Kyiv. A win for Yotova would give a boost for Radev, who also advocates dialogue with Moscow. Victory would make Yotova Bulgaria’s first elected female president. Her main challenger is Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, who is polling at 28-31%. Gyurov, 50, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition, is an outspoken critic of Radev's foreign policy and strongly supports the Euro-Atlantic ties of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state. As caretaker prime minister, Gyurov signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv. The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%. Yotova (R) appointed Gyurov (L) as caretaker premier, a post he held from February to March 2026 Image: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance Altogether 27 pairs of candidates for president and vice president are competing in the first round, with nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin. Top rivals vote, turnout low After casting her ballot in Sofia, Yotova called for peace, stability and unity, urging an end to divisions among Bulgarians. Her main challenger, Gyurov, voted in Blagoevgrad, calling for a Bulgaria that looks ahead and offers families greater economic security. Turnout was estimated at 15.1% by 3 p.m. local time (1300 GMT), according to polling agency Myara, Bulgarian media reported. To win outright, a candidate must secure more than half the valid votes, with more than half of eligible voters taking part. Otherwise, the top two candidates advance to a runoff on November 1. What are the main issues in Bulgaria's presidential election? The war in Ukraine triggered by Russia's unprovoked invasion is one of the central themes in the election, particularly after four merchant ships were allegedly hit by drones off Bulgaria's coast this month in suspected spillover from the conflict. The attacks have prompted Bulgaria to seek assistance from its allies to strengthen maritime security. Satellite internet antennas from the Starlink network — an important part of Ukraine's defense capabilities — were also set on fire near the capital, Sofia. While Radev has said that the attacks seemed to be to the advantage of Russia and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government has declined to blame the incidents directly on Moscow. The strikes have nonetheless raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict. Rising energy prices and inflation that have caused economic hardship to many in Bulgaria, the EU's poorest member state, are also a main issue addressed by candidates. Many voters are also looking to stop government corruption, a persistent concern in the country, and hope for a stable government after multiple elections and coalition breakdowns in recent years. title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
body: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax By Ben Chu Policy and analysis correspondent Published 25 October 2026 We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget. That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing. Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around £24bn to as low as £11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors. The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track. At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance. Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources. BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money , external on Wednesday. 1. Increase taxes on banks Banks in the UK have seen profits rise in recent years because they have been able to charge people higher interest rates when borrowing money. And there is widespread belief among bank bosses that the chancellor is preparing to raise taxes on banks in this week's Budget. Think tank Tax Policy Associates estimates , external that increasing the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax from 3% to 5.5% could potentially raise an additional £1bn to £2bn a year for the Treasury. A higher tax would initially reduce the profits that banks have to distribute to their shareholders. Some shareholders will be wealthy investors. The banks have warned that additional taxes could deter them from investing in the UK , external , which could reduce jobs. And ordinary savers could be indirectly affected too, if their pension investments include bank shares , external . Banks could also pass some of the tax burden on to their customers by offering lower savings rates or higher borrowing costs, research suggests. , external 2. Higher taxes on gambling machines Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown has called on Healey to hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of £500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling. The Social Market Foundation (SMF) think tank has estimated , external that doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise between £275m and £460m - depending on how gamblers reacted to it. People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them. Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels. The gambling industry has argued , external such a tax hike could cause betting shops, which own and operate the machines, to close down, by making them less profitable. It has also argued that betting shop closures could reduce the money bookmakers contribute to horse racing , external , potentially putting jobs in that industry at risk too. 3. Get online marketplaces to collect VAT Reports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by retailers selling on their platforms. The Treasury estimates it is missing out on around £12bn a year , external in VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap". Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full £12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government. Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses. Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities. Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around £1bn in extra VAT a year. Amazon, which supports the move, has estimated it could raise £700m , external a year in VAT for the government. Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers. However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not. 4. Cut welfare spending The above three tax measures together would raise a maximum of only around £3.5bn a year. That would be small relative to the sums of money the chancellor might well need to restore his headroom and pay for any new spending. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in the summer he wanted a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK's welfare bill, while the government is under pressure from opposition parties to find savings from working-age benefits. The Conservatives claim they could make savings of £36bn a year by restricting people's access to welfare payments. Reform say they would save £50bn a year in this way, although independent analysts say there are questions about how realistic it is to make such large savings. Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic and the overall cost is projected by the Office for Budget Responsibility to increase from £68bn this year to £81bn in 2031. Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves attempted to reduce spending on these benefits , external by £5bn a year by 2030, but were forced to reverse course after a revolt by backbench Labour MPs. Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury. Cuts to health and disability welfare would reduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments , external and/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty. However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise. Graphics by Callum Thomson and Lewis McBlane. title: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
body: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap? Image source, Reuters Image caption, A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strike By Tiffany Wertheimer Published 25 October 2026 Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet. Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network. That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people". Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X , external : "Violation of those terms will result in end of service." He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately". How Starlink works on the battlefield Published 15 October There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation. France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus. The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029. For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death. "God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line." For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones. Figure caption, Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Why does Starlink dominate in Ukraine? Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years. Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks. "You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations. Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored , highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate. "Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted. Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk. While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS. "This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control." Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/ Getty Images Image caption, Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink terminal on the battlefield Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree. Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said. The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone. Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company. They are also about five times more expensive, she added. What can the EU offer right now? Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC. She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon. Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted , external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable. Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC. Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom. But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for. That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, French President Emmanuel Macron, with a Eutelsat terminal, at the International Paris Air Show last year Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive. Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve". No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield. But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage." Iris² - The EU's future network Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris² , external is up and running in 2029. The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared ) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one. Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE. It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen. "Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites." Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid". Image source, Paul Hennessy/ Getty Images Image caption, A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying 56 Starlink satellites takes off from Cape Canaveral in March 2023 A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity." So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea. "Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity." It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare." But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war." Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE , external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences. And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases. Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need " a lot of money". Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years. "Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained. Why Space is the new defence frontier Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare. "Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now." While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels. "In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said. Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko Related topics Ukraine Internet More on this story Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role Published 16 October US senators call for investigation into Ukraine's Starlink restrictions Published 16 October
retained_feed_body: Ukraine needs another satellite internet service, but a decent alternative to Elon Musk's network doesn't exist - yet.

title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
body: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates Image source, Reuters Image caption, An Israeli army vehicle passes near the closed entrance of Hebron, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank By Chris Graham and Tom Bennett , Reporting from Jerusalem Published 25 October 2026 All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements. The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory. The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday. It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas. Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed. The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced . Image source, Reuters Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which has led to at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened, according to footage shared online. Even before the entry and exit bans on workers were announced by the IDF on Sunday, the military had cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents. It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment. Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, just days ahead of Israel's election taking place on Tuesday. In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, Netanyahu threatened a "very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory. Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was being "driven by the elections" and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far right and the settlers. On Saturday, thousands gathered in Tel Aviv for a large anti-government demonstration. The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by militants on 7 October 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack. "Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry," the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally. The gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu. Related topics West Bank Israel Israel & the Palestinians Palestinian territories Benjamin Netanyahu More on this story How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders? Published 8 hours ago How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election Published 3 days ago

title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
body: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections Figure caption, Watch: US midterms are 'last best chance to rein in' Trump administration, Obama says By Max Matza Published 24 October 2026 Updated 25 October 2026 Former US President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections. "This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration's immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters "we're in the golden age of America". The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans. Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump. Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members while speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, at one point mocking the president's attempt to redecorate the White House. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, 'enough is enough'," the former president said in Cleveland. Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy. "If you thought everything was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump without using his name, "everything is more expensive now". What are the US midterms? A simple guide Published 6 October Who will win the midterms? Published 16 October Trump, meanwhile, acknowledged that oil prices were "temporarily high" but said "our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are going to come down". The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower fuel prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Talking up the economy, Trump told the crowd in Perry "we're taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs" and repeated his pledge to offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress. He also took aim at the Democrats, telling the crowd they would "loot your wealth" and "annihilate your borders". Using derogatory language, he accused the Democrats of trying to open up immigration from Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia - countries which he described as "terror-infested". Describing a previous meeting with several senators, he recalled: "I said, 'Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from, like, well... Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?'" Image source, Reuters Image caption, Trump cast his ballot in West Palm Beach in Florida on Saturday, before going to support Republican candidate Mike Collins in Georgia In Ohio, the current president faced an attack from his predecessor over the war in Iran, with Obama telling Democrat supporters the conflict had given Tehran "veto power" over the Strait of Hormuz. When asked about the war earlier in the day, Trump said: "I've done it very effectively and I may have to finish it off, or maybe they'll make a deal, but I'm not sure. Either way, we win." He was also asked whether Melania Trump would would visit Ukraine after the White House announced she secured a ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city. "We will see," he said. 'What's with all the gold?' At his afternoon rally, Obama also took a swipe at Trump's efforts to renovate the White House. "What's with all the gold? He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory," Obama joked. Obama's rally in Ohio was to show support for ex-Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running to unseat incumbent Republican Senator John Husted, and Amy Acton, who is running for state governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. Obama criticised Ramaswamy for a campaign ad released last week in which Acton's estranged mother was featured calling her a liar. The ad didn't mention that the woman's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child. Figure caption, The rise of AI election ads in US midterms campaign "In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross. No low he will not sink to try to get in the limelight," Obama said. "I mean, think about this latest ad he ran." Acton also spoke at the campaign rally before Obama to argue that Ramaswamy "has chosen to exploit my childhood" to "save his struggling campaign". Related topics US midterm elections 2026 United States More on this story 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother Published 3 days ago
