title: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future - BBC
body: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future BBC Ultra-Orthodox conscription debate ignites Israel’s election battleground Al Jazeera Will Israel's 2026 election end haredi IDF draft evasion? The Jerusalem Post ‘National suicide’: The election issue tearing Israelis apart SMH.com.au Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics The Conversation

title: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
body: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future Published 25 October 2026 By Sebastian Usher Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police. The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service. The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed. This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050. As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service. Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ultra-Orthodox Jews have staged many protests against being drafted into the military National security and the economy are two of the key issues this election. That means the division between the ultra-Orthodox and the majority of Israelis who believe they are not contributing their fair share to either is starker than ever. With no outright majority likely for any current political alliance, and the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in doubt, the role of smaller parties - including Haredi parties - will once again be crucial in deciding who will govern Israel. To have any chance of staying in power, Netanyahu needs to keep the ultra-Orthodox parties on side, however much pressure there is within Israel for their special status to be diminished. A group apart From the ultra-Orthodox perspective, their social contract with the Israeli state is increasingly coming under pressure. Their all but exclusive focus on the study of Judaism's religious texts - such as the Torah, the Jewish Bible - means their education system is separate and many Haredim are not part of Israel's workforce. For the ultra-Orthodox, the biggest issue of all is holding on to the exemption from serving in the IDF for students at traditional religious - or yeshiva - institutions. This dates back to the earliest days of the Israeli state when the Haredim were a miniscule community of survivors struggling to rebuild from the near extinction of the Holocaust. But as Israel has become more embattled after the attacks of October 7, fighting wars on several fronts, their near complete absence from the country's conscription army has become more controversial. Religious students and their rabbis believe that if young ultra-Orthodox men enter the military, they will be exposed to influences and behaviours that may decisively turn them away from their community. Beyond that, they believe that their staying true to the traditions of their community is vital for the very survival not only of Israel but the Jewish people. When asked not long after October 7 why the ultra-Orthodox didn't contribute more to the military in such an emergency, one of the community's most senior leaders, Rabbi Dov Landau, said that not only should religious students not serve in the army, but they shouldn't even visit the wounded or attend the funerals of soldiers. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The Haredi birth rate is higher than in the rest of Israeli society The rabbi said that in a time of such danger, only Torah students could protect Israel spiritually. "Salvation only comes through Torah learning, orderly Torah learning. And any neglect of or disruption to Torah learning, woe and alas for what will happen… The more Torah learners multiply, the more Torah learners increase their learning, the better. They protect us." It would be a considerable understatement to say that this view is not shared by wider Israeli society. Polls have shown public support for conscripting the ultra-Orthodox surge throughout the war in Gaza. Many see it as a dereliction of responsibility by the Haredi community, made all the more galling by the fact that such a stance comes at the expense of taxpayers. The IDF has bemoaned a deficit in manpower, while many Israelis have had to serve hundreds of days in the past three years. Dahlia Scheindlin is a leading political consultant and pollster in Israel. She says this issue is critical for Netanyahu and is key to understanding this moment in Israeli society against the backdrop of the war in Gaza, particularly among the political right. "Really the most burning, more immediate issue is the right-wing communities who are furious at the government for protecting the blanket exemption from the IDF at a time when, especially among the right, but really everybody in the Jewish community in Israel, is serving and many dying in these wars." Two years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that the exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from serving in the military was effectively null and void. That could have meant that those dedicated to full-time religious study would now be drafted. The reaction from the Haredi community was one of fury. Hundreds of thousands of Haredim held protests, blocking the main highways. And as with the incident in Modi'in, they tried to prevent the arrest of religious students for evading conscription. Protests have continued off and on, and densely-populated Haredi areas are often the backdrops for confrontation with the security forces. Consequences at the polls This is a row that is playing out in the election. There are two parties that have traditionally represented the Haredi community. One is United Torah Judaism – or UTJ – and represents Ashkenazi Jews, or Jews of European origin. The other is Shas, which was formed later and represents the Sephardi and Mizrahi – Jews from North Africa and the Middle East. They share a core agenda, which puts religious study above all else, including any questions around relations with the Palestinians. Both UTJ and Shas have been part of Netanyahu's coalition - and they used their political clout to find ways to try to block enforcement of the Supreme Court ruling. On several occasions, they threatened to pull out of the alliance and bring the government down. UTJ acted on this but continued to support the government from outside, while Shas remained within the coalition. Centre-right politician Gadi Eisenkot, who's shaped up as Netanyahu's main rival in this month's election, does not support their stance. He has made clear his belief that the idea of the ultra-Orthodox constituting a separate state within Israel with its own rules has become increasingly toxic. "A country that sends its best sons and daughters to fight and sacrifice their lives cannot tolerate a reality in which a state within a state exists," he said. All this has meant that the issue of conscription exemption for ultra-Orthodox men is the number one priority on the electoral agenda of both Shas and UTJ. A recent remark by a UTJ parliamentary candidate, Eliakim Stark, has raised the temperature further. He compared the plight of ultra-Orthodox men evading the military draft to the persecution of Jews during the Holocaust. It triggered furious rebukes from opposition leaders from across the political spectrum. Daniel Goldman, an activist who specialises in Haredi issues, says that the two main Haredi parties feel increasingly embattled and less open to compromise. Image source, EPA Image caption, Protesters have blocked key highways He says the ultra-Orthodox don't believe that the state really needs their boys to bolster numbers. "It's at least partly down to the fact that the Haredi parties see the state as wanting to take their boys out of the community and change them from ultra-Orthodox to either regular religious or secular, God forbid, as they perceive it," he says. "And so in that environment of tension, they've actually hardened their positions." Yitzhak Goldknopf from the UTJ, a former minister, has gone so far as to issue an ultimatum: "The Haredim will not change their way of life because there is an army and a war... If there is no choice and they must leave the country, they will leave." But this is having a clear impact on the electoral fortunes of the Netanyahu coalition - of which Shas in particular has long been a key part. Without them, Netanyahu's alliance would fall short of the more than 60 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset. Dahlia Scheindlin, the Israeli pollster, says that the refusal to give up the draft exemption by Shas and UTJ is damaging Netanyahu's coalition. "It is one of the main reasons why the coalition is unable to win back the kind of support that they had in 2022 when they won 64 seats," she says. "They're currently polling at about 50 to 52 seats." All Netanyahu's challengers advocate for ending the ultra-Orthodox exemption and cutting funds to institutions or individuals who refuse the draft. On the left, Yair Golan has called for an immediate mobilisation of those who are eligible. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Benjamin Netanyahu is relying on Haredi support which may not materialise So, despite statements from Shas and UTJ that they would switch allegiance from Netanyahu if he were to dilute his support, there seems for now nowhere else for them to go. Anshel Pfeffer has been a leading commentator on the Israeli political scene for years - now mainly as the Economist's correspondent in Israel. He says Netanyahu's position looks shaky. "There are two things that are bringing together the current opposition bloc," he says. "One is obviously they want to replace Netanyahu and the other is they are capitalising on this really hostile environment nowadays towards the ultra-Orthodox, mainly over the issue of the draft to the army. "Netanyahu has been willing for many years, to basically give the ultra-Orthodox whatever they want. They're not going to get that from the opposition." A potential compromise? Into this arena of resentment and intransigence, a new Haredi party has emerged this year, presenting itself as a break with the traditional mindset of Shas and UTJ. Essentially, the Haredi Public Party is offering a compromise in which the ultra-Orthodox would contribute more to Israel as a whole while maintaining the core of their identity. For the first time in the ultra-Orthodox community, it is also fielding two female candidates. One of them, Ziva Ginz, explained to the BBC her party's position on the military draft. Key to it is men serving being allowed to remain culturally Haredi. "Anyone whose life is genuinely devoted to full-time Torah study should be able to continue learning. Everyone who isn't sitting and studying for a full day should serve alongside the rest of Israeli youth, in frameworks where a young man can enter as a Haredi and finish as a Haredi," she says. But it may be too soon for such efforts at compromise to make an impact this election. Anshel Pfeffer says that it's difficult to sway the base vote in the ultra-Orthodox community, where most still essentially follow what their rabbi says they should do. "And once people are voting for other parties, they won't necessarily do so for another Haredi party," Pfeffer explains. "That's why we're seeing people like [far-right leader and National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir making inroads in the Haredi community, because he's the only non-Haredi party leader who actually talks to young Haredi. Basically, every other party in Israel doesn't even try." Image source, EPA Image caption, Ben-Gvir is making inroads with Haredi voters This is reflected in the polls, which show his Jewish Power party is making gains. If Ben Gvir's actions are increasingly seen as tainting Israel's international image with his support for policies such as annexing the occupied West Bank, his hard-right message is attracting a bigger core of support within the country. His ultra-nationalist ethos is not one that traditionally overlaps with policies of the Haredi parties, but they share a position on the right of Israeli politics. So for some ultra-Orthodox voters looking for a new political home, Ben Gvir represents the nearest alternative. His self-portrayal as a strong man unafraid to take an extreme position against those he perceives as Israel's enemies in the face of international condemnation may attract some already leaning to the far right in the Haredi community. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Gadi Eisenkot has been firm in his support for Haredi Jews serving in the military No alliance appears close to achieving a majority, however, so there is bound to be a lot of horse trading to secure a workable coalition after the vote. Netanyahu will naturally apply his exceptional political skills to trying to find one way or another to stay in power. As ever, that leaves the smaller parties with the ability to play the role of kingmaker. That's a role that the ultra-Orthodox parties have been known for in the past. But this time they may not be the decisive factor. "The truth is, any small party can become a kingmaker," Dahlia Scheindlin says. "I don't think it would take too much to lure the Haredi parties away from Netanyahu... The thing is, though, I don't think the opposition parties will want to lure them in unless they have some promise that they're really prepared to make serious concessions on the draft. The opposition parties are absolutely staking their platforms and their promise to the voters on that issue." This time, rather than being the kingmakers, it may turn out that the ultra-Orthodox parties help bring down the king. Brazilians are choosing between Brazil's current left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin. Americas correspondent Ione Wells reports from Rio de Janeiro as voters choose between two very different candidates. title: Fireworks and tear gas as protesters and riot police clash in Paris
body: Fireworks and tear gas as protesters and riot police clash in Paris Fireworks and tear gas as protesters and riot police clash in Paris Close Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday. A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as protesters were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police. Around 70,000 officers were deployed across France for a second consecutive weekend and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds. The Interior Ministry estimated around 400,000 people took part in Saturday's demonstrations, with nearly 1,000 arrests made. Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Paris, where he says there are few signs the unrest will ease soon. title: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis
body: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Vanessa Trump and her 19-year-old daughter Kai By Grace Eliza Goodwin Published 24 October 2026 Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year. Trump, 48, who has five children with US President Donald Trump's eldest son, said that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free", in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account. Vanessa and Kai Trump then released a longer video on Saturday, in which they discussed breast cancer awareness, early detection and prevention. Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods. "October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram. "I sat down with my mum and Dr Nicole Saphier to talk about my mum's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection." Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from US singer and media personality Mary Millben. Vanessa Trump explained in the YouTube video that she experienced arm pain for several months before discovering a pea-sized lump in her breast, which testing confirmed was a cancerous tumour. "It's a process you have to deal with," she said of the days spent waiting for her test results. "You have to be mentally strong for yourself because you're going to need the strength to fight whatever challenge it is that's coming towards you." Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team. She eventually had a lumpectomy and radiation treatments, she said. The average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%, according to the American Cancer Society. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, it says. Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some cancer cells remain, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk. Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy. title: Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse with five still missing
body: Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse with five still missing Image source, EPA By Aleks Phillips Published 24 October 2026 Two people have been pulled alive from the rubble of a building that collapsed in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, as a search continues for five still missing. Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets on Friday. Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops at the base of the building. The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya. Police said on Saturday that a manhunt had been launched for the building's owner and the contractor responsible for the site. The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors. Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening. He had said on Friday that seven people had been reported missing and rescue teams had made contact with some of those trapped beneath the rubble. The two survivors rescued on Saturday have been taken to hospital, police said. Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath. Image source, UGC/AFP Image caption, Footage taken from nearby shows moments before (left) and moments after (right) the building collapsed Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations. Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday. The National Police Service said it had launched an investigation to establish the cause of the collapse and determine whether anyone was criminally liable. It warned that anyone found responsible for negligence or violating building regulations would "face the full force of the law". Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied. He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards". Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors. Related topics Kenya Nairobi More on this story Search for Nairobi collapse survivors Published 30 April 2016 Five reasons why buildings collapse Published 5 May 2016

title: Turkey's new deal on Mediterranean maritime boundaries with Libya is exacerbating issues with Greece and the EU
body: Politics Turkey Greece protests Turkey-Libya deal on Mediterranean maritime corridor Thomas Latschan 10/24/2026 October 24, 2026 Turkey and Libya plan to redraw maritime boundaries in the Mediterranean as part of a new economic corridor. This has sparked strong protests from Greece, and has also drawn the European Union into the conflict. https://p.dw.com/p/5ObZL Turkey seeks to strenghten ties with Libya in a bid to extract gas from the eastern Mediterranean in future Image: ADEM ALTAN/AFP Advertisement On Tuesday, the parliament of Libya unanimously approved a maritime agreement with Turkey to establish a direct maritime economic corridor between the countries. Turkey had agreed on the corridor with the UN-recognized Government of National Accord in western Libya in 2019. However, the agreement faced opposition from the rival Libyan government in the country's east. Now, though, the eastern parliament has reversed its previous opposition. The decision, which was welcomed by Turkey's Foreign Ministry, is likely to contribute to tensions with other countries in the eastern Mediterranean — especially Greece . Ties between Turkey and Libya have improved through joint projects Image: DHA 'Null and void' The agreement establishes a direct maritime corridor between the southern coast of Turkey and the northern coast of Libya. Large oil and gas deposits have recently been discovered in the region in question — estimates suggest that natural gas reserves worth several hundred billion US dollars may lie beneath the seabed. Turkey and Libya aim to secure their economic rights to these raw materials and are seeking to jointly exploit the resources. The planned corridor disregards Greek islands such as Crete, Karpathos and Rhodes. Greece's government insists that it possesses a comprehensive exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, around these islands and has already announced its opposition to the accord. In a post on X, the Foreign Ministry announced that Greece firmly rejects the agreement and has the support of the European Union in doing so. "The European Union has described the Turkish-Libyan memorandum as null and void, stressing that it violates the sovereign rights of third states and is not consistent with the Law of the Sea," the ministry posted. Similar wording came straight from Brussels. "I raised yesterday's Libyan vote on a maritime MoU with Türkiye and stressed that it infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states," Kaja Kallas, the European Union high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, posted on X. International maritime law Whose claims are legitimate in the eastern Mediterranean is the central point of contention. Greece primarily cites the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS . According to Article 121 of the convention, inhabited islands that "support an economic life of their own” have the same rights to an EEZ as the mainland. This applies to Crete, Rhodes and Lesbos. Athens cites precedents such as a 2022 ruling by the International Court of Justice that found that Colombia had violated the sovereign rights of Nicaragua by authorizing fishing activities in the Central American country's EEZ. The ICJ found that when interests overlap a fair demarcation must be reached that takes coastlines, geographical conditions and the implications of a potential boundary into account. Turkey's government argues that the geography of the Mediterranean plays a special role: If every small Greek island off the coast of Turkey and Cyprus were granted a full EEZ, Turkey would be largely cut off from access to the open sea. This, the government argues, must be given greater consideration when demarcating the boundary. Unlike Greece, Turkey has never signed UNCLOS. Therefore, it does not agree to have the dispute heard by a UN arbitration tribunal. Moreover, even international experts on the law of the sea disagree on what a "fair division” might look like in this specific case. Hifter reversed his position on the deal after opposing it for years Image: Abdullah Doma/AFP/Getty Images Turkey and Libya When Turkey pushed for the agreement in 2019, a brutal civil war was still raging in Libya. At that time, Turkey intervened militarily in the west to support the government in Tripoli, thereby repelling the offensive by eastern Libyan General Khalifa Hifter. Since then, the relationship has changed fundamentally: A successful charm offensive by Turkey's government appears to have led to a political rapprochement with Hifter and his camp. Turkey's government now maintains mutually advantageous relations with both parts of Libya. In addition to the countries' plan to develop energy resources in the Mediterranean together, Turkish construction companies have secured contracts worth billions in recent years for Libya's reconstruction. Furthermore, the Turkish state-owned oil company TPAO and the Libyan National Oil Corporation are already working on joint plans for seismic surveys off of Libya's coast. Turkey's government has established itself as a new military partner for Hifter's forces , supplying weapons and offering training programs. In doing so, Turkey is pushing back against the influence of Egypt and Russia in eastern Libya and strengthening its role as a geopolitical player in the region. How Turkey quietly became a power broker in Africa To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video With the agreement now approved in the regional parliament, eastern Libya also aims to secure its share of the lucrative natural resources. This could give Hifter greater international influence in the future. Disputes in the eastern Mediterranean are likely to escalate further as a result of the agreement — particularly once Turkey and Libya begin extracting oil and gas from the disputed maritime area. The agreement also jeopardizes a major project that is still in the planning stages: the EastMed pipeline, which is intended to transport natural gas from Israel and Cyprus via Greece, thereby making an important contribution to energy security in the European Union. However, the corridor established by Turkey and Libya cuts across the planned route of the pipeline. Turkey has also argued that projects involving cables or pipelines on its claimed continental shelf require its consent. In the long term, this could lead to a division of the eastern Mediterranean region into two competing energy and defense blocs: The Turkey-Libya axis might be countered by an EU-supported alliance of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt and Israel . This article was originally published in German. Advertisement

title: Piero Cipollone: Interview with Milano Finanza
body:
Interview with Milano Finanza Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Piero Cipollone Member of the ECB's Executive Board INTERVIEW Interview with Milano Finanza Interview with Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, conducted by Roberto Sommella on 21 October 2026 24 October 2026 Mr Cipollone, you have just attended a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Italian Banking Association. Was the digital euro one of the topics discussed? We mainly talked about tokenisation. On the subject of the digital euro, I provided an update on the status of the debates on the legislation in Brussels and on the progress of our internal preparations within the Eurosystem. Since you joined the ECB, payments have become one of the main focus areas of your work. Why are they so important for Europe’s future? Because payments constitute a strategic infrastructure for Europe and, as a central bank, ensuring the smooth functioning of payment systems falls within our mandate. Whenever we buy something online or pay for a coffee, we think about the price of what we’re buying. But we hardly ever think about how the payment is made. Yet if the payment system stops working, the economy stops working. Will the introduction of the digital euro help with this? Yes. Today we can use money issued by the central bank only in the form of cash. But a growing share of our economic life takes place online, where banknotes can’t be used. The digital euro fills this gap. It gives people the freedom to make payments using an instrument that is equivalent to cash in terms of its nature and characteristics, such as privacy and covering all payment needs, but which also works where cash can’t be used. Why has this now become necessary? Ever more purchases are being made online. In Italy, for example, according to the latest available data, online payments grew from 6% of the total in 2019 to 24% in 2024. And I expect they’ve grown even more since then. These online purchases are normally made via card payments and two thirds of these payments are made using non-European card schemes. For most euro area countries, this dependence on non-European operators is not limited to online payments but also extends to physical shops, because they don’t even have anything like Italy’s Bancomat that would enable payments to be made in local shops. In short, for an essential service like payments, we are heavily dependent on an infrastructure over which we have no direct control. So can the digital euro be described as a European digital sovereignty project? The Eurosystem focuses on matters that are closely related to its mandate. And, as I said at the start, the smooth functioning of payment systems is one of our responsibilities. If we are critically dependent on third parties, it’s not easy to ensure this smooth functioning. In recent years Europe has learned that, for some essential services, we cannot rely only on third parties. We saw this with energy and we’re seeing it today with defence. And the same is true for payments. The digital euro will give Europe an alternative of its own, bringing to the digital world what cash has always ensured: a secure form of public money that protects privacy and is accepted throughout the euro area. Sovereignty doesn’t mean shutting third parties out. It means having the power to choose and knowing that, for an essential service like payments, Europe can also rely on its own strength. Does this dependency bring any specific consequences for merchants too? Yes, particularly for small merchants. Today the fees that a small shop pays can be up to four times higher than those paid by large operators. The digital euro will introduce a European alternative that will increase competition and, thanks to the caps on costs laid down by law, will help to reduce fees for those with less bargaining power. From this perspective, it seems that there’s no time to waste. Absolutely. In 2027 we will already launch a pilot based on real transactions carried out by the staff of the ECB and the other national central banks. It will serve to test the technology in real conditions and to build the digital euro hand-in-hand with the market. 36 market operators, of which seven are Italian, are already collaborating in the preparatory works. And we are now calling for e-commerce and mobile commerce operators to take part. If the regulation is approved this year, the digital euro could be rolled out as early as 2029. When will the final decision be taken? The decision can only be taken once the legislative negotiations that are under way in Brussels have been concluded. We hope that the regulation will be adopted by the end of the year, enabling the ECB’s Governing Council to issue a formal decision on issuance. The adoption of the regulation will make it possible to complete the rulebook with the technical rules necessary for the market to prepare ahead of time. The ECB can get the infrastructure ready, but banks, payment system operators and merchants will also need time to adapt their systems and processes. Will there be a limit on holdings of digital euro? Yes, but there won’t be limits on payments. The limit applies to how much digital euro I can hold in a digital wallet, not how much I can spend. If a payment exceeds the available balance – when buying a car, for example – it will be possible to take the remainder automatically from the linked current account. The limit on the amount of digital euro that can be held will safeguard financial stability, particularly in crisis situations. Our analyses show that with a properly calibrated limit, there will be no negative effects on the banking system. Is it true that it will also work offline? Yes. It will be possible to make payments in shops during a power cut or in remote and isolated areas where there’s no internet connection or where the connection is weak and sporadic. It will suffice to bring two devices together, as when using a contactless card today. The payment will be made directly between the payor and payee, without going via the internet. It means merchants can keep receiving payments even when other digital payment methods are not available. This will make the digital euro more resilient and will also better protect privacy. With offline payments, details of the transaction remain exclusively between the payor and the payee, very much like cash payments today. How exactly will we be able to use the digital euro? Will a new app be available? There will be two options. Banks will be able to integrate the digital euro into the apps their clients already use, while the Eurosystem will offer an easy-to-use, standardised, reliable app with the basic functions. Even if you use the latter option, your relationship will nevertheless still be with your own bank; the ECB will not open accounts for people. But what will this European app be used for? Just as banknotes are the same throughout the euro area, the digital euro app will also offer a common point of access. The digital euro must be accessible to everyone, regardless of their country, their age or their digital skills. We have incorporated accessibility from the design stage onwards, and have been working with organisations representing those with disabilities. We are implementing a clear principle set out in the European Commission's legislative proposal, i.e. the choice of how to access and use the digital euro should remain in users’ hands and not be controlled by payment service providers. Will the ECB decide how much digital euro will be issued, based on a limit set each year, just like it does for banknotes and coins? No. As is the case for cash, it will be up to citizens and firms to determine the digital euro’s use based on demand. On which technological platform will the digital euro run? It will run on a common European infrastructure developed exclusively by European providers, on which banks and private operators will be able to build new services. We’ve already seen this in our innovation programmes: more than 70 operators worked with the ECB to explore the options the digital euro offers to provide new services to their customers. Some firms have already put forward solutions, such as automatic digital receipts or automatic payment upon delivery for online purchases. These are tangible innovations that will make life easier for people and firms. We have just launched a second call for new ideas and projects, with the aim of speeding up innovation and creating new growth opportunities for the European payments industry. Banks have complained because they are afraid of being left out of the digital euro loop. Are their fears justified? Dialogue with the banking sector has been, and continues to be, an essential component of the project. The digital euro has not been devised as a replacement for banks, but to integrate and strengthen their own payment services. It will in fact be the banks and other authorised intermediaries that will distribute the digital euro, manage customer relationships and develop new services. The digital euro’s common standards will enable payment solutions developed in Europe to reach customers and merchants throughout the euro area. Is it conceivable that one day there will only be the digital euro? I don’t think so, and I don’t think that’s what anyone is aiming for. The goal is to create a payment system in which cash, the digital euro and the services already offered by banks coexist in such a way that resilience will be guaranteed and consumers will have freedom of choice. How can cyberattacks be prevented? The digital euro’s security will be built on multiple layers: advanced encryption, data segregation and regular testing for simulated attacks. The infrastructure will also be distributed across several European regions to ensure continuity of service even if part of the system were to become temporarily unavailable Security is not an afterthought, but an integral requirement built into the project from the very start. We can draw on the Eurosystem’s wealth of experience in managing critical infrastructure such as TARGET. Will we be able to buy everything with the digital euro, such as a coffee, a government bond or even a share? The digital euro will be a means of payment, not a tool that the ECB will be able to use to tell people how to spend their own money. People will be able to use it to buy a coffee, shop online, pay a bill or even transfer money to somebody else. In short, the digital euro will be available for in-store, online and person-to-person payments. The ECB is a federal institution. What is still missing from the European Union for it to become truly complete and stronger from a financial perspective? Europe already has a single currency and a single central bank. Now we must complete the process through the creation of a genuine European capital market, a more integrated banking system and common infrastructure in strategic sectors. Today, Europeans' savings far exceed the financing needs of our firms, but a significant portion of those savings ends up outside Europe, while many European firms struggle to find the capital they need to grow, innovate and compete. We need to find a way of ensuring European savings do more to finance the European economy. A start-up or an innovative small business should be able to access not just capital from its own country but available capital from anywhere in Europe with ease. To achieve this, there is work to be done on several fronts, including legal, regulatory and technological. On the technological front, we have a real opportunity: new technologies such as distributed ledger technologies (DLTs) allow us to overcome the fragmentation of market infrastructures. The Eurosystem is making a concerted effort towards this through the Pontes project, which went live on 21 September 2026. It enables the settlement of financial transactions carried out on DLT platforms using central bank money. Its complementary project, Appia, aims to create a fully integrated European financial ecosystem. The common theme is the same as for the digital euro: we have a single currency, but in many sectors we still have fragmented national markets and infrastructures. Completing the European capital market would mean that citizens and firms could truly take advantage of the opportunities offered by a market operating on a continental scale. title: Why Russia's arrest of Japanese journalist is the latest sign of deteriorating ties between the countries.
body: Politics Japan Japan-Russia ties erode as journalist sits in Moscow jail Julian Ryall in Tokyo 10/24/2026 October 24, 2026 Japan is demanding access to a journalist who was arrested by Russian security services. The Kremlin claims that Japan is using journalists as spies. https://p.dw.com/p/5OanL Journalist Yuki Imai  seen being taken into custody by Russian security agents Image: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement Japanese Foreign Ministry officials were in Moscow this week in an attempt to contact a journalist arrested in Russia's far east on allegations of spying . Journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on October 14 by Russia's FSB security service in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island. Televised footage of the arrest showed FSB officers barging into his hotel room as he slept. The correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was accused of attempting to obtain information on soldiers in the region, which is near the Kiril islands, a geopolitical sore spot in Russia - Japan relations. Russian authorities quickly transferred him to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held in pretrial detention until at least December 12. If convicted, 34-year-old Imai faces up to 20 years in jail, according to the International Federation of Journalists, which has called for his immediate release. Officials from the Japanese embassy in Moscow have been denied access to Imai. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the arrest and dismissed the claim that Imai was a spy. Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev said Imai had been caught "red-handed," the official TASS news agency reported. Nozdrev has claimed that Japanese intelligence agencies use journalists to collect classified information with the goal of "undermining Russia's security and defense capability." Russia accuses journalists of being 'spies' Yoji Gomi, a veteran journalist and author who has reported from across Asia, told DW that Japanese journalists may occasionally meet with diplomats in the course of their work and "share thoughts and impressions." However, he rejects the idea that reporters are paid spies. "One-party nations often see foreign correspondents as spies because that is exactly what they use their journalists for," he said. "I can completely see how the Russians decided that Imai was a spy, as it is how they operate, plus he was in a sensitive part of Russia where there are lots of North Korean laborers that they want to keep quiet," Gomi added. Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo's International Christian University, told DW that Russia might see Imai as a bargaining chip it can use to exchange for nationals detained overseas. Nagy doubts that Japan will give in to pressure. "They are going to resist because it means that Russia, or any other country, can then just seize a Japanese national, put them on trial for espionage and demand the release of one of their people," he said. "It would set a dangerous precedent," he added. The arrest comes after a member of the Russia-linked hacking group Qilin was arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany to face charges in connection with a 2024 cyberattack on a logistics center. The last time a journalist was arrested in Russia was in 2019 for "attempting to obtain classified information about Russia's military potential in the Far East," Russia's Interfax news agency reported. However, in this case, the journalist was quickly released. Imai's case is perhaps the most serious since 2023, when Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony before being released in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024. Russia has previously arrested foreign journalists for prisoner exchanges. US reporter Evan Gershkovich is seen here in a Moscow court. Image: Dmitry Serebryakov/AP/picture alliance Strained Japan-Russia ties Imai's arrest is the latest in a series of incidents that have sent bilateral relations into a tailspin . Nagy said Imai's seizure was designed to put pressure on Tokyo. He added this is part of a coordinated approach with China to isolate Japan at a time when the US is preoccupied with domestic issues and the conflict in the Middle East. "Moscow and Beijing are coordinating to create the image that Japan is not a reformed member of the international community but still the military state of the 1930s and that it poses a threat to stability in the Indo-Pacific region," Nagy said. "This is all designed to smear Japan's efforts to lead diplomacy in the region at a time when the US is perhaps distracted," he said. "And it does not even matter much that it is not true; they will just continue to repeat the claim to discredit and weaken Tokyo." Decadeslong row over disputed islands Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Sophia University, told DW that he believes Japan had been working hard to maintain a stable relationship with Russia, even after Tokyo joined international condemnation of the invasion of Ukraine . Anno said Russia's timing in turning up the heat on Japan was puzzling. "Japan condemned the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because it was a fundamental violation of international law, but Russia is only now pushing back hard," he said. At the center of deteriorating ties is a territorial dispute about a chain of islands off the far north of Japan that were seized by Soviet forces after Japan's surrender in World War II. There had been hopes in the past in Tokyo that a concerted diplomatic effort could be sufficient to convince Russia to return the islands — known as the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia — to Japanese sovereignty. That campaign has faltered in the past couple of years, and was further dented when Japan announced in the spring that it would be joining the NATO initiative to provide nonlethal assistance to Kyiv. In August, President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed islands , becoming only the second Russian leader to do so. Earlier this month, a delegation of Chinese businesspeople was welcomed on one of the islands, and talks are underway on the possibility of economic cooperation. Edited by: Wesley Rahn Advertisement

title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
body: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Canada and the US are currently locked in a tit-for-tat trade war By Nardine Saad Published 23 October 2026 Updated 24 October 2026 The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change. From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday. Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry. The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August. Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers". Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports. The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products". It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade". Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Maine Senator Susan Collins is seeking to keep her seat in November's midterm elections Trump "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce", White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said. Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests." The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term. Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner". The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts Published 31 August She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers". Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire." Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war. Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state. Also on Friday, Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US. Carney, who has sought closer ties with Europe since the tariff war erupted, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but was willing to wait it out. "We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that." LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada. Related topics United States Canada Trade war Trump tariffs US midterm elections 2026 More on this story US embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midterms Published 4 days ago

title: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?
body: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires? Image source, Reuters By Sareen Habeshian Los Angeles Published 24 October 2026 Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions, and being home to the rich and famous. Now voters are about to decide whether the mega-rich among them - including media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian, and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare. Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires. There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted". What are the US midterms? A simple guide Published 6 October But the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has roiled politics for decades. "I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap. The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps. Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system. Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill . "If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC. Image source, Getty Images While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports , external . California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue. A September poll , external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided. The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents. California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year. While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs. Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue. In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022 , external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland , external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%. GUIDE: What are the US midterms? IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians EXPLORE: How the US midterms will be won and lost VERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under Trump NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax. They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey. Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax. "I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he said, adding that the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly  given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn. DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state". Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax Published 3 days ago Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said , external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believed the way the measure was written was "problematic", it was necessary to protect vulnerable Californians. Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy. "I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief said in an interview with the BBC's US partner CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream." Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40. While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th Century, that they have a God-given right to rule". "They have all the wealth, they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on November 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles. Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels , external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California. Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey , external from the Public Policy Institute of California. Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment" driving the policy. "This is really not about Prop 40," he says, but rather about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit". Correction 24 October: An earlier version of this article contained a graphic which incorrectly said median income in California was $288,000. This has been corrected to median household net worth. title: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
body: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election Image source, Guy Delauney/BBC Image caption, The Student List is Number 3 on Serbia's ballot paper, so the figure seen being hugged by this supporter has become a symbol of the movement's fight for change By Guy Delauney in Belgrade Published 24 October 2026 If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race. Ilija Srdanović appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans. He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to Vučić since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012. The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad. What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election Published 2 days ago Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list. "It is absolutely normal to stand with my students to help them in their fair struggle," Srdanović told the BBC. Image source, Guy Delauney/BBC Image caption, Ilija Srdanović tops the Student List's 250 candidates but would not necessarily lead Serbia if they won The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month , he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister. Whatever Vučić's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge – an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media. He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure. Vučić has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally. Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history. Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A reported 150,000 supporters turned out for the final Student List rally in Belgrade's Slavija Square on Thursday night Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won. Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time." The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness. "We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name. "All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds. The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage. At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources". The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Vučić continues to command strong support among sections of Serbia's population For the past 18 months, there has also been a full-time, pro-SNS camp in the small park between the National Assembly and the Presidency building in the centre of Belgrade. Its residents have repeatedly attacked journalists and made the park a no-go zone for local people. Vučić has called the camp "a symbol of resistance" against those who "cannot stand different opinions". But his major challenge remains what happened outside Novi Sad railway station two years ago. The station's renovation was a key part of his signature infrastructure project – the high-speed line linking Belgrade and Budapest. So it has been difficult for Vučić to distance himself from the disaster. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Aleksandar Vučić stepped down as president last month with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands". "This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED. "Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy." On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act. Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia. Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power. "When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally. "You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart." The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar Vučić as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates. The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader – or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer. Related topics Serbia

title: Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?
body: Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Close Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky says unexplained limits on Starlink and Starshield services continue to affect Ukrainian forces, while US officials and Elon Musk offer conflicting accounts of who controls the restrictions. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones. The BBC's Washington correspondent Daniel Bush looks at what officials have said about the technology. title: Trump's approval rating on economy hits all-time low as midterm looms: CNBC survey
body: Trump economic approval hits new low before 2026 midterm election Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Economy Trump's approval rating on economy hits all-time low as midterm looms: CNBC survey Published Thu, Oct 22 2026 7:40 AM EDT Updated Fri, Oct 23 2026 4:49 PM EDT Steve Liesman @steveliesman WATCH LIVE Key Points President Donald Trump's economic approval rating is hitting an all-time low, according to the latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey, with 65% of Americans saying they disapprove. Economic pessimism among Republicans has risen sharply in recent months. With the midterm election approaching, the survey of 1,000 registered voters found Americans prefer Democratic control of Congress by a 52% to 45% margin, a 3-point gain for Democrats since the July survey. watch now VIDEO 6:04 06:04 Trump’s approval rating on economy hits all-time low as midterm looms: CNBC survey Squawk Box With less than two weeks to go before the congressional elections, Americans are nearly as gloomy about the economy as they were when the nation was emerging from the pandemic, and President Donald Trump 's economic approval rating is hitting an all-time low, according to the latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey . Eight out of 10 Americans rate the economy as fair or poor, the highest number since December 2023 and one of several ominous signs for Republicans in the new polling data released Thursday that show why their candidates are facing an uphill battle in the midterm . Downbeat views on the economy are most intense among Democrats and independents, but there's been a strong move toward economic pessimism even among Republicans in recent months. Overall, 63% of the public is pessimistic about the current state of the economy and the outlook, up 1 percentage point from the July survey . But that percentage now includes 35% of Republicans, up 6 points from July and the highest level of Republican pessimism of either of Trump's two terms. "We got there not because of independents or Democrats getting more sour — it's because Republicans have," said Micah Roberts, partner at Public Opinion Strategies, the Republican pollster for the survey. "Since Trump has been president, [Republicans] have held on to a small margin saying that the current economy is either excellent or good. And now that has kind of broken and changed." The survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1%, found Americans preferring Democratic control of Congress by a 52% to 45% margin. The 7 percentage point Democratic edge represents a 3 percentage point gain for Democrats from the July survey. The poll contained other foreboding signs for Republicans as well. It showed 72% of Democrats highly interested in the midterm election on Nov. 3, compared with just 62% of Republicans. Women are 10 percentage points more interested in the election than men, and they prefer Democratic control of Congress by 22 points. Independents prefer Democratic control by a wide 49% to 33% margin. And the majority of survey respondents said Democrats would do a better job than Republicans on many of the issues they singled out as their top concerns, including corruption and the cost of food and gas . Read the full survey results here. In the eight states with competitive Senate races, respondents prefer Democratic congressional control by 4 percentage points. Trump carried those eight states by a combined 10 points in the 2024 presidential election. The survey shows "things moving either away from Republicans or toward Democrats, depending how you want to look at it, in a way that would make me very nervous if I was leading Republican campaigns leading into these last two weeks," said Jay Campbell, partner at Hart Associates, the Democratic pollster for the poll. Despite the economic gloom, Trump's overall approval rating has remained stable, though at just 40% approving and 59% disapproving. His current net approval of -19 percentage points compares with -8 a year ago. More striking is the sharp 9-point drop in the president's net economic approval rating from just the last survey in July. The president's economic approval fell to 34% from 38% in three months and disapproval rose to 65% from 60%. The net -31 economic approval is the lowest of either of Trump's two terms. The 65% disapproval rating is 1 percentage point higher than former President Joe Biden 's worst showing and the highest for any president surveyed by CNBC going back to President Barack Obama . Government corruption was identified as the top concern by 36% of respondents, and Democrats hold a 4-point lead on addressing the issue. On the cost of food and groceries, the second-most important issue, the Democratic lead widened to +16 from +7 in the July survey. Democrats also topped Republicans on protecting democracy as well as dealing with the high price of gas . Among those most interested in the election are respondents who identify corruption and protecting democracy as top issues, and they prefer Democratic congressional control by wide margins. Republicans continued to hold a strong advantage on border security and immigration, but the lead on immigration fell to +9 from +15. Democrats, meanwhile, are seen as better at handling the issues of jobs and unemployment and Iran, which flipped from +2 for Republicans to +5 for Democrats. Read more about the CNBC All-America Economic Survey Trump’s approval rating on economy hits all-time low as midterm looms Corruption is voters’ top issue ahead of midterm election Trump is pushing a massive AI buildout. His own voters are wary of what comes with it America by the numbers: How voters feel about the economy, inflation and Trump The public continued to be skeptical of the value of the Iran war. The survey found just 46% of the public believe the military action was worth it to disrupt development of Iran's nuclear capabilities, down from a 53% majority in April. And just 35% say the military action was worth it given the rise in the price of gasoline. While the survey showed continued deep divisions by party, there was near unity on the corruption issue. Ninety-three percent said elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should not be allowed to personally own or trade stocks in individual companies that have contracts with the federal government. And 89% said companies owned by or invested in by a sitting president's immediate family members should not be allowed to receive contracts from the federal government. While corruption was a top issue, prices are clearly top of mind for registered voters. Taken together, concern about the cost of food, gas and housing is the top concern for 57% of respondents. Eighty percent say prices are rising, up 5 percentage points from a year ago, with 55% saying they are rising faster than usual, also up 5 points. The cost of food actually eclipses gas as a greater concern in the survey 34% to 23%. It's a top worry among most major demographic groups but is most elevated among those making $30,000 or less and supporters of the agenda of Democratic Socialists of America. Yet it's also the top issue for those Republicans who don't count themselves as MAGA supporters. Both pollsters were cautious about how extensive Democratic gains could be. Roberts from POS said it's a battle between "the map and momentum." "There are several indications nationally that the electorate is tilting more toward Democrats … but the movement is also fairly concentrated, each party's base is consolidating, and a 'big change' is dependent on Democrats flipping a lot of districts and states that Trump won handily just two years ago," he said. Campbell doesn't see a "realignment" election like in 1994 and 2008, saying, "This looks like a return to the mean—young voters and voters of color returning to the Democratic fold, bolstered by independents being fed up with Trumpenomics." He adds, "At no point did anyone expect that Democratic candidates would suddenly pull 15% of the Republican vote."
